rows.title: Global bond sell-off pushes 10-year Treasury yield to highest since 2002
rows.content:
Emily Herbert and Ian Smith in London, William Sandlund in Hong Kong and Leo Lewis in Tokyo

Published October 1 2026

Updated October 1 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

A global bond rout briefly pushed US Treasury yields to their highest level since 2002 on Thursday while Eurozone borrowing costs surged, as pressure from the Iran war energy shock on public finances intensified around the world.

Yields on 10-year Treasuries climbed as much as 0.05 percentage points to 5.34 per cent, a level last seen almost a quarter of a century ago, as traders warned the $32tn US government bond market, an anchor for global finance, was caught in a “vicious loop” of selling. They later rallied to 5.24 per cent, down 0.05 percentage points on the day.

Meanwhile, UK 30-year gilt yields climbed above 6 per cent for the first time since 1998 but later eased to 5.93 per cent.

Traders had been “dazzled” by the scale of the recent government bond sell-off, said Rob Subbaraman, head of global macro research at Nomura, adding that this was driven by higher inflation and concerns about the sustainability of government deficits.

The surge in yields has swept across the global economy , raising borrowing costs for consumers, businesses and governments. US conventional 30-year mortgage rates jumped 0.25 percentage points — the biggest increase in four years — to 7.28 per cent this week, according to Freddie Mac data released on Thursday.

Investors have warned that jumps in yields in recent trading sessions have been exacerbated by hedge funds and other big investors, which have been forced to ditch long-term debt to counteract the effect of rising rates on their broader debt portfolios, or to unwind lossmaking trades as the market has sold off.

Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, was up 3.2 per cent to $101.15 a barrel on Thursday, adding upward pressure to yields.

Mike Bell, head of market strategy at RBC BlueBay Asset Management, said: “You’ve got to a position where lots of people are getting stopped out of long positions or thinking: I don’t want to hold this as [the yield] keeps going up.”

On a choppy day for Eurozone bond markets, France’s 10-year yield rose as much as 0.1 percentage points to 4.96 per cent on Thursday, touching its highest level since mid-2002 in intraday trading.

The swings came as the French government put forward a 2027 budget with €43bn of cuts and tax increases amid rising worries over the health of its public finances.

The euro dropped as much as 1 per cent to a 16-month low of $1.1216, buffeted by higher oil prices and what analysts said were rising risks from the bond market sell-off. European bank shares fell, with BNP Paribas down 3.6 per cent and Deutsche Bank falling 2.6 per cent.

Italy’s 10-year government bond yield was up 0.05 percentage points to 4.69 per cent, taking its spread with German debt to 1 percentage point for the first time since March.

Italy and other Eurozone government bonds were starting to suffer from “spillovers” from the French bond sell-off, said Pooja Kumra, rates strategist at TD Securities. “[The] moves have been significant and will need some vocal intervention from policymakers.”

European stocks fell as investors fretted over possible fallout from higher yields. The region-wide Stoxx Europe 600 stock index dipped 1.3 per cent while the FTSE 100 fell 1.7 per cent.

In the US, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 were about flat just after midday. Wall Street stocks have been relatively resilient to the sell-off in debt, buoyed by investors’ bullishness about the AI theme.

Harriet Ballard, a portfolio manager at Aviva Investors, said she remained positive on the equity market, despite the pressure from higher interest rates, because “AI-linked sectors have been better insulated by strong earnings”.

Lifted by rising yields, the dollar was up 0.5 per cent against a basket of its peers to its highest level since April last year.

Bond markets have for months been racked by fears over the spectre of higher inflation triggered by the Iran war’s energy shock, which has pushed the relationship between oil prices and Treasury yields to its tightest point since 1990 . This has been intensified by robust US economic data, which has further fed expectations of higher interest rates.

Traders are braced for further swings, with the Ice BofA Move index of implied volatility in Treasuries approaching the high reached in the first weeks of the conflict.

As the bond worries spread through Asian markets earlier, Japanese 10-year bond yields rose 0.04 percentage points to 3.1 per cent, close to a multi-decade high.

Mitul Kotecha, head of Asian foreign exchange and emerging markets macro strategy at Barclays, said the pressure on Japanese bonds was down to “a combination of the contagion of what’s happening in the US market and, to some extent, uncertainty about [the Bank of Japan] tightening [rates]”.

“It’s the fiscal concerns that continue to play in the market,” he added.

Corporate credit spreads have also widened in recent days as investors worry that the volatility in government bond markets could spread into the credit markets that determine companies’ borrowing costs.

The additional interest rate paid by European investment-grade companies over government bond yields has ticked higher to almost 0.9 percentage points this week, the highest level since April, according to ICE BofA data.

“There is a risk that credit spreads follow [yields higher],” said Andrew Jackson, head of investment at Vontobel Asset Management.

Inflation data in several European countries — including Germany, France and Italy — on Wednesday showed higher price pressures than analysts had expected, adding to investors’ fears that the energy price shock is feeding through into economic strain, although US data showed a drop in the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation measure.

Investors have been struck by a relentless march higher in global bond yields where problems in each market, including Japan, France and the US, are feeding off each other.

“As [yields] move up, they are pulling each other up,” said Guy Miller, chief market strategist at Zurich.

rows.title: Burnham criticised over support for Manchester City owners
rows.content:
Lucy Fisher in London

Published October 1 2026

Updated October 1 2026

Downing Street has sought to downplay Andy Burnham’s backing for the owners of Manchester City, after the Conservatives accused the prime minister of politicising the Premier League’s investigation into the club.

Burnham said on Wednesday that he would be “really concerned to lose” the club’s owners, whose roles have been thrust into doubt after it was found guilty of more than 100 breaches of financial rules.

He praised the City Football Group, which is controlled by UAE vice-president Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, for having been “such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester” during his time as mayor of the city region.

The Conservatives said the government “must keep politics out of football”, and accused the prime minister of being “out of touch” with football fans who were “horrified” by the allegations against City.

Downing Street issued a statement on Thursday clarifying that “the initial judgment is serious and there can’t be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules”.

Pointing out that Burnham had “stressed that it is an ongoing independent process”, a Number 10 spokesperson said: “If wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences.”

City have vowed to appeal against the Premier League panel’s findings, including that it artificially inflated its revenues by more than £900mn over nine years.

The episode has fuelled questions about whether the league’s enforcement of its financial rules could damage a crucial UK economic and diplomatic relationship.

Quizzed about the dilemma, Burnham acknowledged the matter could also affect both the Premier League and “brand UK”, adding that it needed to be handled “carefully without everybody jumping in and providing their conclusions”.

Recalling the dispute in which Everton, whom he supports, were found to have breached the Premier League’s financial rules in 2023, he insisted his club “weren’t treated fairly”.

He told ITV he had been “really dissatisfied with the nature of the process that had been conducted when Everton was finding itself part of an independent commission”.

Ahead of the Tory annual conference in Birmingham starting on Sunday, party leader Kemi Badenoch predicted that Burnham “is going to call an election sooner than he is saying” and speculated a poll could be called as early as next May.

Reflecting on his plans to launch a national care service, reform Britain’s electoral system, and revisit the UK’s relationship with the EU, Badenoch told BBC South East: “All the policies he announced are for after an election, so if he’s not calling an election why is he talking about things happening in 2030?”

rows.title: Train driver accelerated through red signal before fatal crash
rows.content:
Robert Wright in London

Published October 1 2026

Updated October 1 2026

The driver of a train involved in a fatal rail crash in Bedfordshire received an automated warning that he was passing a red signal but still accelerated before hitting another train stopped on the track, an interim report has revealed.

However, the report by the Rail Accident Investigation Branch, published on Thursday, also found the signal, near Elstow, issued a false danger warning to the Nottingham to London train that was hit in the collision on 19 June, which caused it to halt.

Following the crash, the signal had issued a second false danger alert to another train on 9 July, the report said.

The crash killed Shaun Burton, the driver of the Corby to London train that passed the red signal, and injured more than 160 people. The incident, on the Sheffield to London Midland main line, was the first fatal collision on the UK’s railways since October 2024.

The revelation that the antiquated automatic warning system (AWS) failed to prevent the crash is likely to lead to renewed calls for increased use of the train protection and warning system (TPWS), which automatically applies the brakes of any train passing a signal at danger.

TPWS was widely fitted at junctions, terminus stations and other places posing a high risk of collision in the early years of the 21st century following a series of serious crashes caused when drivers failed to respond properly to AWS warnings.

However, for cost reasons, TPWS was not fitted at locations judged lower risk such as the signal that Burton’s train passed.

An initial report published days after the crash found that Burton’s train — which investigators identified by the code 1H46 — had passed a red signal that should have protected the stationary Nottingham to London train on the track ahead. But investigators had not yet established whether Burton had correctly received an AWS warning.

Thursday’s report used information from the on-train data recorder (OTDR) — or “black box” — of the Corby to London train.

AWS issues drivers a warning if they pass signals showing red or yellow lights, but they only apply the brakes if the driver fails to acknowledge the warning within 2.7 seconds.

The report said: “The OTDR from train 1H46 recorded that the driver acknowledged the AWS warning indication, but the train continued to accelerate towards and beyond the signal, which it passed at 17:12:53.”

Burton applied the emergency brakes about 10 seconds before the impact but succeeded only in slowing the train from 75mph to 50mph.

The Nottingham to London train, meanwhile, had been forced to stop after its driver failed to respond within the required 2.7 seconds to a false AWS danger warning from the signal that Burton’s train subsequently passed at danger.

Further investigations were needed to establish why Burton did not respond correctly to the AWS danger warning before the crash, the report said.

The Department for Transport said it would ensure the rail industry acted on any findings in the RAIB’s full report when it was published.

It added: “The interim report makes clear there is still much to be established about the incident and we urge people to refrain from speculation until the full facts are set out.”

This story has been updated to correct details of AWS danger warnings

rows.title: EU countries in crisis talks over release of diesel stocks
rows.content:
Ian Johnston and Henry Foy in Brussels and Anne-Sylvaine Chassany in Berlin

Published October 1 2026

Updated October 1 2026

Could you be the FT’s top trader?

European countries are in crisis talks over the release of diesel stocks, as the US threatens them with a diesel export ban unless they release strategic reserves of the oil product.

Three people familiar with the matter said the US administration had put pressure on European countries to release strategic stocks of diesel, warning that it could ban US diesel exports if they do not do so.

The EU’s energy commissioner Dan Jørgensen had held talks with officials from France, Germany, the UK, Italy and Ireland on Thursday, in an attempt to co-ordinate and develop a joint response to the threats from Donald Trump, an official said. No decision was taken on a release, they added.

“We are in very close contact to co-ordinate with our member states how we go forward and we have on a separate track also high-level contacts with the US administration on this,” said Anna-Kaisa Itkonen, a spokesperson for the European Commission. These were “intense contacts given the ongoing situation”, she added.

A Trump administration official told the FT: “It is in Europe’s best interests to work with the United States as we pursue multiple pathways to boost the supply of refined products and lower costs for consumers.”

Trump is under intense pressure to lower prices at the pump ahead of US midterm elections. The US oil industry has urged the president’s administration to ask European allies to release diesel stocks as part of a frenetic lobbying campaign in Washington this week aiming to prevent a US export ban.

One person in the industry told the FT that Europe may hold up to 400mn barrels of diesel in commercial inventories and stockpiles, which, if released, could bring down global prices.

The oil industry has told the Trump administration that a diesel ban would undermine its efforts to promote the US as a reliable energy exporter and could backfire by pushing up prices of petrol and other products.

Donald Trump says he is still considering if to bring in a diesel export ban

Members of the International Energy Agency in March agreed to release 400mn barrels of emergency stocks globally to calm oil markets. At that time, Europe said it would release 32.7mn barrels of government stocks and 74.8mn barrels of industry reserves, 70 per cent of which were oil products. The Americas provided 172mn barrels, with the US releasing the remainder of its stocks on Tuesday.

Announcing the release, US energy secretary Chris Wright said: “While the United States and Japan are delivering on their commitments, several European member countries have released only a fraction of the crude oil and petroleum products they pledged. We urge every member country to fulfil its commitments.”

Fatih Birol, head of the IEA, said on Tuesday that some European countries had not yet released all the stocks they had committed to in March. “The countries have already made major efforts in Europe. A big chunk of the stocks have been released, but still some remain, both in terms of crude oil and products,” he told journalists.

Earlier on Thursday, Reuters reported that the US administration wanted the EU to release 120mn barrels over six months.

“The US is pressuring Europe to release more of their reserves which are heavily weighted towards diesel, with 195mn barrels on paper,” said analysts at consultancy Energy Aspects.

“However, we believe governments are unlikely to release all pledged volumes too hastily or at once, given the uncertainty surrounding the ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and between Russia and Ukraine. They know releasing the [strategic reserves] will be the last bullet in the chamber.”

Bob McNally, founder of energy analysis group Rapidan and a former adviser to George W Bush, said: “European countries have not complied with their pledged strategic stock releases, which include diesel fuel. If Europe steps up on pledged diesel stock draws, the US may step back on restricting exports.”

A German official said the country had received “no new requests from the IEA” to release reserves. “As a general rule, the market must not be destabilised,” the official cautioned.

Additional reporting by Jamie Smyth in Washington and Malcolm Moore in London

rows.title: BT seeks government nod for potential TalkTalk takeover
rows.content:
Kieran Smith in Brussels

Published October 1 2026

BT has opened talks with UK government officials over the possibility of a takeover bid for struggling rival TalkTalk, as the country’s largest broadband provider prepares a late entrance into the auction for the heavily indebted company.

Allison Kirkby, chief executive of the FTSE 100 telecoms group, this week met officials at the Department for Culture, Media and Sport to seek assurances that a takeover of TalkTalk would not trigger an in-depth antitrust review, according to three people familiar with the matter.

BT is interested in buying the company’s wholesale and retail businesses, two of the people said.

Its broadband network Openreach, which is deemed by industry watchdog Ofcom to have significant market power, is TalkTalk’s largest supplier. The division covers more than 30mn UK homes, almost 25mn of them with full fibre.

People familiar with the TalkTalk auction said that it had been held up partly by other bidders’ concerns over the quantum of fees payable to Openreach.

Meanwhile, BT is also the country’s largest broadband provider with 30 per cent market share, according to estimates from Enders Analysis.

BT is working with antitrust lawyers at Clifford Chance on the possible TalkTalk deal, some of the people said.

TalkTalk’s owners, which include founder Sir Charles Dunstone and private capital group Ares, have been seeking a buyer for the troubled business for months. The company was previously in exclusive negotiations to offload its wholesale business to Octopus Investments and its consumer operations, which serve 1.6mn customers, to Opus Broadband.

However, neither party has been able to reach an agreement, forcing TalkTalk to explore options including a break-up that would potentially carve up the company between private capital group Epiris and Ares, its largest creditor. Talks with several potential buyers are ongoing, according to one of the people.

The company’s existing shareholders have been forced to inject money into the business to cover shortfalls on several occasions.

BT is hoping to have gained enough clarity over the antitrust situation to be able to make a decision over a deal for TalkTalk by the weekend, one of the people said.

Karen Egan, head of telecoms at Enders Analysis, said that “when companies get to the level of distress that TalkTalk appears to be in, competition concerns tend to take a back seat.”

“In this instance, the government will be more concerned about security and continuity of service for vulnerable customers,” she added.

TalkTalk has struggled since it was taken private by Toscafund, a London-based hedge fund, in a £1.1bn leveraged buyout in 2021 that added £527mn of debt to its balance sheet. The company’s retail customer base has fallen from more than 2.5mn in 2023 to about 1.6mn in May.

Shareholders injected £235mn into TalkTalk as part of a refinancing in December 2024 and then a further £120mn in July last year. Ares pumped in another £115mn in March.

A DCMS spokesperson said that “this is a commercial matter and we do not comment on speculation”.

TalkTalk, BT, Ares and Epiris declined to comment. Clifford Chance did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Additional reporting by Jim Pickard in London

rows.title: Dealmakers line up to test EU’s appetite to create European champions
rows.content:
Barbara Moens

Published October 1 2026

For companies, bankers and corporate lawyers around Europe, there is a sudden scramble under way to recast how they pitch a series of big mergers and acquisitions to regulators.

The EU is signalling that it is opening the door to bigger corporate mergers, allowing European companies to gain the scale needed to compete with Chinese and American rivals.

So in response, companies and their advisers are framing their planned deals as test cases for this new approach, betting that arguments about the need for European champions, resilience and investment will help win approval.

Several potential contentious transactions in industries ranging from mining to elevators — and one including a satellite tie-up between Airbus, Thales and Leonardo — are set to provide first indications in the coming months of whether the change in language translates into a more permissive approach to consolidation.

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen has emphasised the need for European champions and cast competition policy as an important part of the bloc’s competitiveness agenda. Meanwhile, her competition chief Teresa Ribera has been explicit in saying the new approach does not amount to a blank cheque for consolidation.

For businesses, that unusual divide over policy leaves one crucial question: how much will actually change?

“Businesses and investors need to see a body of coherent precedent showing how the framework will operate in practice, and it’s for businesses and advisers to work constructively with the commission to achieve this,” said Rafique Bachour of law firm Skadden Arps.

That body of precedent does not yet exist. So, as one Brussels-based M&A-lawyer, points out: “Every big case will now be packaged differently and presented as a test case to create a European champion.”

There is no shortage of candidates. The proposed joint venture between paper manufacturers UPM and Sappi has left the commission concerned it will restrict competition in the markets and give the companies the ability to increase prices. However, the companies argue the deal is the only way to stay competitive and maintain the security of supply in a shrinking industry grappling with excess capacity.

Anglo American’s planned sale of its Brazilian nickel assets to China-backed MMG is seen as a test of how far Brussels is willing to go in its stronger China policy. The case ticks boxes for both resilience and security of supply.

Further down the pipeline is a bid by Finnish lift maker Kone to buy its rival TK Elevator, a deal that from a traditional antitrust perspective would be seen as a steep uphill battle. Whether European competition officials will now assess it through a different lens will be closely watched by dealmakers.

But the clearest test of Brussels’ new philosophy is emerging in space. Airbus, Leonardo and Thales want to combine their satellite business in a venture designed to create a European player capable of better competing with Elon Musk’s SpaceX. Its competitors warn it would weaken competition, ultimately increasing costs for taxpayers.

The mix of traditional merger policy, industrial policy and geopolitical competition makes the joint venture, dubbed Project Bromo, “the obvious test case and a no-brainer”, another lawyer said.

In unusually public remarks about an upcoming antitrust review, von der Leyen referred to the Bromo merger in a recent speech and said “these are the types of industrial champions we need if Europe is to lead in the space economy of tomorrow”.

Ribera subsequently defended the independence of European antitrust officials, many of whom are already nervous about the new political winds. The Spanish competition commissioner made clear that von der Leyen’s comments did not mean “we are not going to apply and to enforce our own regulation”.

Some antitrust experts argued von der Leyen should have given her political steer more subtly. But for companies and deal markets, more clarity is welcome.

That is acknowledged by some European Commission officials, well aware their in-tray is being closely watched. “We need one deal that shows we are serious about the shift,” said one.

rows.title: Do US lawmakers finally have capital in the crosshairs?
rows.content:
Oren Cass

Published October 1 2026

The writer is an FT contributing editor and chief economist at American Compass

Greed is so often the undoing of an otherwise brilliant scheme. Never satisfied, people become overconfident, push the envelope too far. And everything comes tumbling down. The high-flyers of finance seem headed towards a similar fate, as capital’s share of US income continues to rise, its share of tax payments continues to fall, inequality worsens, wealth concentrates and deficits become unsustainable. All the while the financial engineering gets ever more absurd.

For just one example, take AQR, the hedge fund behind a fairly recent innovation in tax avoidance called the “tax-aware long-short” account, which wraps leveraged, straddled portfolios around conventional equity indices or established fund strategies to generate large harvestable losses and indefinitely defer taxation on gains. Close to $200bn has poured into the strategy at AQR and its imitators such as Quantinno , which welcomes investors “to the next evolution of tax-loss harvesting” and has seen its assets swell from $2bn to $70bn in just a few years.

Such elaborate gamesmanship helps some of America’s highest earners to reduce taxes on even their wage income . The Financial Times reported earlier this year that fathers at a local sports game in Greenwich, Connecticut, “were fixated on AQR’s Delphi Plus fund, which specialises in ordinary income losses”.

The extraordinary wealth that these individuals and their money managers had already accumulated wasn’t enough, nor was the favourable tax treatment afforded to their capital gains, which in effect meant they might be able to pay a lower share of their income in taxes than their secretaries did. They had to avoid paying taxes altogether, and then claim this as the righteous course.

AQR chief Cliff Asness has said that the moral issue here is that of working for a client’s interests. But things are surely not that simple. A fiduciary duty to a client requires putting his interest above any other, but it does not require pursuing every potential action or developing every potential product.

The ethical business owner or manager operates within not only the letter but also the spirit of the law. It is the letter that determines whether a punishable violation has occurred. But as Milton Friedman observed in his famous essay arguing that “ the social responsibility of business is to increase its profits ”, the “basic rules of the society” include “both those embodied in law and those embodied in ethical custom”. Ethical custom may be a more subjective matter, but a good place to start is with the easily discernible intent of the laws established through the democratic process.

The defenders of the latest “tax-aware” funds make a comical effort to equate the exotic manoeuvres with garden-variety deductions and retirement saving. But the exercise must be enormously complex to justify the huge fees that the funds charge, allowing the financial wizards to pocket a good chunk of the revenue they divert from the public purse. Clearly, they are embarrassed by all this, or at least nervous about the potential consequences.

They should be. The political winds are shifting and even a business-friendly Republican administration is fed up. On Monday, the US Treasury department issued a notice of plans to scrutinise a range of schemes. “Treasury is serious about cracking down on transactions designed to dodge taxes or exploit our federal tax code,” warned Treasury secretary Scott Bessent in a social media post.

Beginning in the 1980s, the US tax code was rebalanced in favour of capital, in the belief that creating better conditions for its holders to deploy it and reap the rewards would ultimately redound to the benefit of all. The theory required some trust that the capitalists would indeed pursue their profit in ways that would be broadly beneficial. Instead, we got a metastasising financial sector dedicated not to productive investment but to helping the rich get richer by moving money in circles, extracting wealth from the real economy and then paying no taxes at all.

The central argument against wealth taxes, high marginal tax rates and taxes on mobile capital is that they will merely fuel avoidance and push productive activity away. But if we get the same with low tax rates, what then? The US is now in a fiscal crisis and capital should expect to find itself in the crosshairs. If the financial sector is determined to be a socially corrosive drag on the economy, then it is going to have to be taxed that way.

rows.title: Accenture shares surge 22% as consultancy confounds AI fears
rows.content:
Stephen Foley in New York

Published October 1 2026

Updated October 1 2026

Accenture shares surged 22 per cent on Thursday after the world’s largest publicly traded consulting group said its revenues could accelerate this year, confounding fears that AI would destroy demand for its services.

The 800,000-person company reported an 8 per cent rise in earnings for the 12 months to August, as it benefited from cost-cutting and said AI was helping it to generate more revenue per employee.

Accenture , whose shares in June plunged to a nine-year low over concerns that AI would crush demand for consultants, reported revenues of $74.2bn for the fiscal year, a 4 per cent increase, after a stronger than expected final quarter.

Julie Sweet, chief executive, said Accenture was taking share from rivals in a difficult market.

“Our clients believe AI will help them achieve more than previously possible across the enterprise but they remain at very different stages of readiness,” she said. “Much of our growth today comes from continuing to build their digital core . . . Many are just starting their AI journey.”

Sweet said the company had allowed staff to carry over unused holiday to encourage them to complete work for clients in the final weeks of the fiscal year.

Accenture said its revenues could increase more quickly in the coming year despite concerns about how AI is disrupting the consulting industry.

The group set a target of 3 to 6 per cent growth for the current fiscal year. Wall Street had been expecting around 4 per cent for the mid-point of the range.

Net income for the fiscal year that ended in August was $8.4bn, up 8 per cent, helped by job cuts and other cost-reduction measures the company took a year ago. In the past three months, however, Accenture added more than 15,000 new jobs, taking its global workforce to more than 814,000.

The share price rise took the consultancy’s market capitalisation to more than $135bn. It had fallen from more than $200bn during a post-Covid consulting boom to less than $80bn earlier this year.

Previous technology revolutions boosted consulting firms, as they won work advising companies on how to adapt. But investors have been fretting that AI may not provide a similar stimulus if clients divert spending to in-house AI projects and expect consultants to complete projects using fewer staff and at lower rates.

Sweet said Accenture would continue to expand entry-level hiring, but the overall growth in employee numbers would slow due to AI.

“We are seeing an increase in revenue per person, which is what you would expect in part due to AI,” she told analysts on a conference call.

Accenture’s shares had fallen to a nine-year low in the wake of the company’s previous quarterly results in June, when it lowered its revenue forecasts, blaming the war in the Middle East and delays to two large contracts. The shares are still trading about 15 per cent lower than at the start of the year, even after Thursday’s rally.

Rival consulting firms have highlighted continuing weak demand in recent months. Deloitte reported last week that tech consulting was its slowest-growing division in the past year.

Accenture’s results were “well above expectations”, said Surinder Thind, analyst at Jefferies. “While overall growth remains tepid compared to historical levels, perhaps most importantly, the guidance suggests it is not deteriorating as AI fears would have you believe.”

rows.title: International Criminal Court cuts ties with Axa over US sanctions
rows.content:
Suzi Ring in London

Published October 1 2026

The International Criminal Court has cut ties with its health insurance provider Axa, as the war crimes tribunal attempts to shield itself from the impact of US sanctions.

The ICC and Axa have terminated their contract effective from October 1, according to The Hague court. President Donald Trump has stepped up attacks on the ICC as reports suggested the US would impose sanctions on the whole institution, adding to existing measures against several people working there.

The ICC opted to end its deal with Axa as both parties feared that new, broad-based US sanctions would force the insurer to stop doing business with the court or face punishment.

Axa has held months of discussions internally and with the court about potential workarounds, but the Paris-based insurer was unable to find a solution without a so-called blocking statute, said a person with knowledge of the situation.

Blocking statutes are legal mechanisms used to shield companies engaged in international trade from being forced to comply with sanctions issued by other countries.

A group of MEPs has been calling for the EU to enact a blocking statute in relation to US sanctions against the ICC, but while there is support among dozens of MEPs for such a measure, no such statute has been enacted.

The ICC — which prosecutes individuals for offences including genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity — has been contending with the latest round of US sanctions for nearly two years. Some 13 court officials, including half of the tribunal’s 18 judges, are currently subject to the restrictions.

US secretary of state Marco Rubio launched a campaign in July to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick”, calling on member states to withdraw from the court, while Trump told the UN General Assembly last week that the ICC was “out of control” and an “evil group of people”.

In an interview last month, deputy prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan — who is co-running the prosecutor’s office after former chief prosecutor Karim Khan was ousted — told the FT that the ICC had taken steps to insulate itself against further US sanctions, “ensuring that we are autonomous for the future”.

The court has spent the past year overhauling its systems , shifting its office software from Microsoft to Germany’s openDesk. Individuals at the court who are subject to US sanctions have faced restrictions on holding US credit cards, purchasing mobile phones and receiving packages via US couriers. They have also had hotel reservations cancelled.

While the US, which is not a member of the court, has long criticised the war crimes tribunal for over-reach, the tension has increased during Trump’s second term. The ICC issued an arrest warrant in 2024 against Israeli leader and US ally Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes in Gaza.

In response to questions about the use of blocking statutes, the European Commission said earlier this week that it was “in constant touch with our member states but diplomatic outreach remains our preferred option”, whilst reiterating its “full support for the ICC’s work and its staff”.

A spokesperson for the ICC said Axa and the court had “decided by mutual agreement to terminate the contractual relationship” and that it would use a new, unnamed health insurance provider.

Axa said: “It is a complex and sensitive case given the risks arising from the extraterritorial application of US sanctions. Situations of this kind, which are extremely difficult for the individuals affected, are relatively new and reflect an international environment that has become increasingly tense and complex for businesses.”

The Republic of Naoero, north-east of Australia — formerly known as Nauru — told the UN last week that it was withdrawing from the ICC. Niger, Burkina Faso, Venezuela, Mali and Chad have also notified the court of their withdrawal this year.

Additional reporting by Paola Tamma

rows.title: UAE investigates if Flydubai attack was ‘terrorist activity’
rows.content:
Chloe Cornish in Abu Dhabi and James Shotter in Jerusalem

Published October 1 2026

Updated October 1 2026

Investigators are rushing to determine why a pilot attempted to crash a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv on Wednesday, with the United Arab Emirates launching an investigation into possible links to terrorism.

The country’s attorney-general Hamad Saif al Shamsi had ordered a probe to collect evidence on the altercation between the flight’s two pilots, state news agency WAM reported on Thursday.

The investigators will look into “the extent to which [the incident] is related to any terrorist activity” and whether the attack was premeditated, according to WAM.

A person familiar with the situation said Israel was also “involved” in investigating the incident but declined to provide further details.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Thursday that the co-pilot who stabbed the aircraft’s captain and attempted to crash the plane had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination”, without presenting evidence for his claim.

“The attacker, the co-pilot who attacked the captain, is now being interrogated, but here’s what we do know. First, we know that he underwent Islamist radical indoctrination. That appears to be something we’re gathering from the information, his personal information,” Netanyahu told Fox News.

He added that it was too early to tell whether the incident was linked to Iran , but that Israel would know “definitively within a matter of days”.

The flight took off from Dubai before being diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia, after the plane’s co-pilot stabbed the pilot and the aircraft plunged 18,000ft within the space of 90 seconds. Passengers and crew struggled with the attacker and managed to land the plane safely.

Netanyahu earlier told CNN that he had spoken to UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan, and that the Emirati leader had “agreed that Israel would join the interrogation”.

Israel’s far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said on Thursday that the government should demand the extradition of the pilot who carried out the attack.

“Anyone who planned to crash a plane and murder 180 Israelis must be extradited to Israel and pay the ultimate price here,” he said in a statement.

Dubai government-owned Flydubai on Wednesday evening said its flights between the emirate and Israel were suspended “while the investigation continues”, without mentioning which authority was leading the probe.

Flights into Tel Aviv — from Israeli airlines and international carriers such as Delta, KLM, Etihad and Wizz Air — continued to run on Thursday, with only a small number of cancellations or delays. So far, carriers have not been asked to make changes to flights or security by Israeli aviation authorities, according to one airline still flying into the country.

The attacking co-pilot’s identity has not been revealed, although Israel has said he is an Omani national. His motivation remains unknown.

The incident has raised questions about the usually rigorous security checks passengers undergo before flying to Israel, which has a history of aviation-related attacks.

Additional reporting by Peter Campbell in London

rows.title: Israel flight near-miss triggers election furore
rows.content:
James Shotter in Jerusalem and Neri Zilber in Tel Aviv

Published October 1 2026

The near-downing of the Flydubai plane carrying 174 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv has triggered a political storm in Israel, with Benjamin Netanyahu’s opponents accusing the Israeli prime minister of exploiting the incident for political gain ahead of this month’s election.

The attack came less than a day after Netanyahu — whose campaign has been dogged by recriminations over the security failings around Hamas’s October 7 2023 attack — issued a vague warning that there were “indications that . . . our enemies will try to attack us” ahead of the October 27 vote.

In the wake of the attack, during which the jet nosedived nearly 20,000 feet after one pilot stabbed the other in an apparent attempt to crash the plane, Netanyahu’s allies sought to portray his warning on Tuesday as a sign of the prime minister’s strong security instincts.

Even before the passengers had returned to Israel, defence minister Israel Katz issued a statement saying: “When the Prime Minister and I issue security warnings and alerts based on intelligence, everyone — including our external enemies and uninformed former officials at home — would do well to listen and take them seriously.”

Yair Lapid, who in his position as leader of the opposition demanded — and was granted — a briefing from Netanyahu on the security threats the prime minister had alluded to, later said Netanyahu did not mention any threat to hijack a plane.

“It is forbidden to say what is said in a security update and I am strict about it, but it is allowed to say what wasn’t said: there was no mention of a plane hijacking scenario. Nothing like it. Nothing. Nada,” he wrote on Thursday.

“The Prime Minister’s Office has become so unhinged and out of touch that they are trying to score political points off the plane incident.”

As the Israeli passengers returned home on Wednesday night, the national mood was one of rejoicing, with news cycles dominated by stories of the heroism of the passengers who overpowered the attacking pilot.

But the near-downing of the plane, which came less than four weeks before Israel goes to the polls, has also become part of a campaign in which security already features prominently.

Most opinion surveys suggest the election is too close to call. Netanyahu’s far-right coalition is trailing a broad coalition of opposition groups. But the gap has narrowed in recent weeks and both blocs remain short of a clear majority.

Netanyahu conceded in an interview with CNN on Thursday that there had been no specific intelligence relating to the attack on the plane.

But analysts said that, in the short term, the incident might be a boon for the prime minister as it diverted the news cycle away from longstanding questions over the lapses that preceded the October 7 attack, which happened on his watch and is widely seen as the worst security failure in Israeli history.

Those questions have dominated the public discourse in recent days following reports that Netanyahu — who has sought to cultivate a reputation as Israel’s “Mr Security” over two decades as premier — received advance warnings from Emirati and Egyptian officials that Hamas was preparing for an attack. The prime minister has vociferously denied this.

“There are less than 30 days until the election. Every day that passes and people aren’t talking about October 7 is good for Netanyahu . . . The less he has to talk about October 7, the better it is for him,” said Aviv Bushinsky, a political analyst who previously served as Netanyahu’s chief of staff.

“It’s much better for him to be talking about brave Israelis.”

Indeed, on Wednesday evening, Netanyahu rushed to greet the returning Israelis as they landed at Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion International Airport. Videos on social media subsequently showed him singing a well-known Israeli pop song about life always getting better during a meeting with one passenger and his family.

Jonatan Urich, an adviser to Netanyahu, accused Lapid and other opposition leaders Gadi Eisenkot and Naftali Bennett of failing to grasp the urgency of the prime minister’s security warning earlier this week.

“Prime Minister Netanyahu said this yesterday,” Urich wrote on Wednesday of the warning. “Eisenkot, Bennett, and Lapid snickered. Today we all saw what happened. It is forbidden to let them lead Israel.”

The longer-term impact of the incident on Israeli politics is expected to depend on further revelations about the motivations of the attacker, whether he acted alone and how he was in a position to carry out his assault. The United Arab Emirates said it was investigating whether the attack was premeditated or connected to “terrorist activity”.

Analysts said that, unless the investigation revealed serious failures by Israeli authorities, they did not expect it to persuade voters in the country’s deeply polarised society to cross the political divide, not least because most had already decided what they thought of Netanyahu.

“We don’t have any way to predict how voters are going to react to the kind of incident they’ve never seen before,” said Dahlia Scheindlin, a pollster and political analyst.

“What we do know from polls is that voters have not changed their minds about Netanyahu. Not for. Not against,” she added. “I don’t think this is going to be the thing that causes voters to cross blocs.”

But Bennett, a former prime minister, argued the reaction from Netanyahu and his “delusional” aides was another reason why he was unfit to lead the country.

“If you suspected there was a danger that planes will explode on us, what did you do? Who did you convene? What did you check?” Bennett said.

“A prime minister is not a siren,” he said. “I don’t need a prime minister to give warnings, I need a government that will protect.”

By Martin Sandbu and Tej Parikh

Published September 25 2026

The global economy is facing another period of uncertainty as conflict in the Middle East and a surge in AI investment add to the pressures created by years of economic shocks and geopolitical upheaval.

What will drive the next stage of global growth? Where are the biggest risks? And how will shifts in bond yields, trade, technology and geopolitics affect businesses and households?

Tej Parikh and Martin Sandbu, answered your questions on the global economy.

This is part of our live Ask an Expert series, giving readers the chance to put their questions directly to FT journalists. For more topics, visit our Ask an Expert page .

For more on the global economy listen to the Economics Show with Soumaya Keynes podfollow.com/economics-show

Answered by: Martin Sandbu Answer: There are a lot of questions on government debt in this Q&A, so it's clearly a source of worry. And the basic numbers don't look good - debt-to-GDP ratios are at or near long-term highs, and many big countries' deficit numbers are not closing.But I'm quite heterodox on this and think we may be worrying a tad too much. Debt-to-GDP ratios are mostly stable at the moment - in part thanks to inflation of course. If deficits are no larger than nominal GDP growth (when debt is around or below 100% of GDP), then the ratio can remain stable for some time. Also note that while western governments are seeing rising debt service costs, the share of GDP they spend on interest payments remains below where it was a decade or more ago. It's not quite don't worry, be happy. But I don't think we should happy.

Second, assuming (quantum based) AGI, can governing become out of human hands?

rows.content:
Abigail Hauslohner in Washington

Published October 1 2026

This is an on-site version of the White House Watch newsletter. You can read the previous edition here . Sign up for free here to get it on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Email us at [email protected]

Hello from Washington and welcome to White House Watch. Here’s what we’re looking at today:

Hegseth announces series of new initiatives in “State of the Force” speech

Trump says Powell should be “forced to resign” from Fed board

White House holds crunch talks on diesel export ban

US defence secretary Pete Hegseth announced the creation of an “Autonomous Warfare Command (Autowarcom)” to spearhead the military’s use of unmanned weapons.

Hegseth is creating the new command at a moment of intense public debate over necessary safeguards for AI, after several recent incidents in which advanced AI models under development went rogue and hacked into outside systems without being instructed to do so.

Hegseth said he expected there to be internal resistance to the creation of Autowarcom, which will operate on the same level as other combatant commands such as US Central Command and US Special Operations Command. The new command will be able to deploy weapons and buy drones and other autonomous systems, something the individual services currently do.

It was one of a series of new initiatives announced by Hegseth during his “State of the Force” speech on Wednesday.

Addressing hundreds of junior officers and enlisted troops at Marine Base Quantico, Hegseth touted his overhaul of the military and its culture, which has included the firing of many of the military’s top ranks, and an expanded emphasis on physical appearance and masculinity.

“The ideological clowns are out. The patriotic cowboys are in, with testosterone testing on top,” he said.

Trump said former Federal Reserve chair Jay Powell should be forced off the central bank’s board even after an investigation into a $2.5bn renovation project found no evidence of criminal wrongdoing.

OpenAI’s software has obscured efforts to scrape data from crucial government agencies , according to new findings that show the scale and severity of AI hacks are far larger than previously known. Meanwhile, a US competition watchdog is expanding its investigation of the AI company.

The US has withdrawn its remaining troops from Iraq, marking an end to more than two decades of US involvement in the country.

Trump has unveiled plans for South Korea to invest $200bn in US energy projects , including eight nuclear power plants, a six-gigawatt power facility and a long-delayed liquefied natural gas project.

US government bonds have posted their worst month in four years as investors warn the world’s most important debt market has been gripped by a “vicious loop” of selling.

What’s inside Silicon Valley’s AI “self-regulation” agreement with Trump? Here’s what to know.

Myles McCormick, Jamie Smyth and David Sheppard exclusively report that Trump’s aides have presented the president with options including curbs on international diesel sales, people familiar with the discussions told them.

Administration officials have also briefed foreign allies including the UK about possible disruption to their supplies.

A White House official said Trump was “evaluating all the options on the table” to lower domestic fuel prices and that no decision had been taken on whether to suspend exports.

The crunch talks come as US oil and gas executives surveyed by the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas found that diesel prices would not return to normal for more than a year . Almost half of those polled expect diesel prices will take more than four quarters to return to 2025 levels, according to the anonymous survey of 100 oil and gas companies.

The president is at the centre of a lobbying fight between Republican allies worried about the political impact of the diesel price surge — which has hammered farmers and other parts of US industry — and oil bosses desperate to preserve lucrative exports.

rows.title: Australia’s banks show how to prepare for cable blackouts
rows.content:
Elisabeth Braw

Published October 1 2026

The writer is the author of ‘The Undersea War: The International Battle for Supremacy at the Bottom of the World’. She is a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and advises M&C Saatchi World Services

Australia is connected to the rest of the world by a rather small number of subsea data cables. Those cables efficiently transmit all the connectivity the country needs; they even offer spare capacity. But if the cables were damaged, Australia would struggle. Now the country is creating a backup that would thwart the worst harm — and other countries should learn from the Australians’ pragmatic take.

Earlier this year, executives from National Australia Bank sat down with managers from other leading financial institutions and government officials. The purpose of the gathering was to simulate what would happen if the country’s subsea cables suddenly became unavailable. “In the first stage, we hypothesised that the cables on the east coast, where most of our cables run, were cut,” Brad Carr, NAB’s executive in charge of geopolitical risk, who conceived the simulation exercise, told me. “And then we assumed the cables on the west coast were cut too.” The teams switched to satellite communications, only to discover that this transmitted a minuscule portion of the data — that is, money — they needed to send.

On their own, satellites won’t save banks or anyone else if cables suffer a massive outage. The Australians realised that they needed to plan for a situation in which their country found itself cut off from the rest of the modern world. Repair ships and their crews excel at their task, but they need time to get to the fault site, and malicious actors could obstruct them. Then there are administrative delays. Repairs to cables that travel through Indonesian waters — including the crucial links that connect Australia and Singapore — require Indonesian permits, which can take over a month to obtain.

For all these reasons, Australia needed a backup plan, the exercise demonstrated. Its major banks had already, together with the government, begun developing a plan that would allow the financial system to work in a mostly offline situation. “If we have a major incident, how can we make sure that our customers can pay for groceries?” Carr explained.

In parallel, the government has launched CI Fortify , guidance for infrastructure operators “in preparation for instances of crisis or service disruption”; it also expects operators to be able to isolate their infrastructure from other networks and systems for up to three months to be able to provide critical services to Australians.

If the cables were cut, the country would have to become digitally self-sufficient, relying on its domestic connectivity. In a crisis Australian consumers would be able to use their debit cards and withdraw cash from ATMs, and banks would be able to make necessary transactions, though without access to international bank-clearing systems. “It’s like field surgery, not a complete hospital,” a person familiar with the efforts told me. “There will be blood, but it will save the patient.”

Finland is making similar advances. And this summer, Sweden’s central bank teamed up with retail banks and payment cards “to enable card payments to be made even in the event of disruptions in data communication lasting up to seven days”.

Australian leaders are acutely aware of China’s fast-growing submarine fleet and the mysterious visits paid by Chinese research vessels to nearby waters. It could be nothing — but if it’s not, Australia will weather the storm a whole lot better than the countries that treat the risk of a major cable incident as unlikely. In August, Vietnam — which was less prepared — faced a major subsea-cable crisis when four of its eight major cables were damaged and connectivity dropped by 30 per cent.

Much of modern life would come to a halt without undersea cables. Planning for the turmoil that would hit the financial system if they were cut creates resilience at little expense.

rows.title: Is circular financing in AI a problem?
rows.content:
Toby Nangle

Published October 1 2026

There are lots of ways in which circular financing among AI companies can be organised. A new report from a team of Bank for International Settlements researchers lists three.

First, there are those tech firms who receive both financing and business from another tech firm; so, maybe including Amazon pouring billions into Anthropic while also supplying the Trainium chips used to train Claude.

Second, suppliers could be financing customers to stimulate demand for their products, a bit like old-fashioned vendor financing. Nvidia’s pivot to providing ‘ balance sheet as a service ’ comes to mind — along with numerous reports of the giant chipmaker pumping cash in the direction of its financially more precarious customers so that they can buy more chips.

Or the flow could run the other way: customers financing suppliers in order to secure critical inputs. And finance can take many forms, from straight-up loans and equity injections through to forward compute contracts. So maybe the $300bn of business with which OpenAI is backstopping Oracle’s data centre build-out counts, even if OpenAI doesn’t actually have the $300bn and is relying on current or future investors to supply it.

Third comes everything else: reciprocal commercial relationships where goods or services flow both ways.

Looking at a universe of 1,246 AI firms split across compute, infrastructure, data tools, models and applications, the report’s authors — Jon Frost, Rudraksh Kansal, Kumar Rishabh, Vatsala Shreeti and Leanne Si Ying Zhang — found, perhaps unsurprisingly, a lot of circular relationships.

Totting up all the incoming investment flowing to AI firms between 2021 and 2025, they reckon more than half came from other AI firms. And looking just at this lump of AI-to-AI deals, almost half of these were between firms that shared some commercial relationship, suggesting “that a significant portion of financing and commercial relationships in AI are self-referencing.”

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

But is it a problem?

... circular relationships make reported demand partly endogenous to firms’ own financing decisions. For example, when a supplier finances a customer, part of the supplier’s revenue growth reflects its own capital investment, rather than organic final demand. This makes it harder for investors, lenders and supervisors to gauge what part of the current AI boom is based on organic demand.

Beyond making analysts’ lives a bit tricky, are there real-life problems for the rest of us?

The parallel with the telecommunications boom of the late 1990s is instructive : upstream equipment vendors such as Lucent and Nortel financed network operators so that the operators could buy the vendors’ equipment. This meant that part of the equipment vendors’ reported sales was being funded by the vendors themselves. For a time, as operators expanded their networks, equipment orders also expanded and vendors booked both the sales and loans as assets. However, when operators’ own revenues failed to materialise or slowed, they could neither repay the loans nor sustain the equipment purchases. Equipment vendors then sustained both financial losses and a loss of sales. Such dynamics may also play out in AI if revenue growth and end user demand fall short of firms’ expectations.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

We couldn’t find a market cap series for Lucent, but the Nortel market cap chart suggests circular financing can be a problem. But is it a problem this time ?

...these circular arrangements tend to be opaque, making monitoring and supervision difficult. Many of the firms involved in AI are private and may disclose limited information. Even where firms are publicly listed, deal terms can often be complex, mixing cash investments with long-term purchase commitments and guarantees on the value of the underlying assets. Residual value guarantees (RVGs) are one example, where the guarantor pledges to cover any shortfall in an asset’s worth (such as chips or data centre equipment) after a fixed period. These contingent commitments sit off balance sheet and only materialise during a downturn – when a guarantor is least able to absorb them. As such, reported deal values may not capture the whole picture, and headline figures can differ substantially from disbursed amounts. Moreover, many of these firms reside in different sectors and jurisdictions, making it difficult for a single supervisor or regulator to monitor these risks.

Hmm. Without the necessary disclosures to pore through, even the hardest-working supervisor or investor is going to struggle to know whether it’s a problem until after the fact.

But there is a silver lining. If it does turn out to be a problem, the BIS reckon that at least we’ll all know about it. Not only through a public equity market swoon, and upending of macroeconomically significant investment. But also because they reckon risks will be magnified by hidden leverage and interconnected exposures across private credit and special purpose vehicles used to finance AI infrastructure. 😬

rows.title: The best art exhibitions to see in London right now
rows.content:
Published March 29 2025

Updated October 1 2026

The Bayeux Tapestry is at once epic and intimate; grandly remote and shockingly close. Its historic loan to the British Museum has resulted in a pitch-perfect installation of this extraordinary chronicle of the Norman conquest. Though conceived as a political creation, its unexpected depiction of the conquest’s civilian victims escapes crude propaganda, while its propulsive narrative power and exhilaratingly cinematic action animate history as few works have since. Read the FT’s full article

Richard Dadd’s first London retrospective in half a century follows the Victorian fantasy painter from his early fairy scenes to the extraordinary works made during four decades in psychiatric hospitals. The Royal Academy offers a persuasive reading of how a schizophrenic artist, through sorrow and kind, individualised treatment, found meaning and beauty in art. Highlights include the dazzling “Titania Sleeping” and the painstaking “Fairy Feller’s Master-Stroke”, whose microscopic detail creates a dizzying visual overload. This small, personal show commemorates a singular talent in British 19th-century art, poignantly unlike anyone else. Read the FT’s full review

Ana Mendieta’s compelling, often very beautiful survey at Tate Modern follows an artist who effaced herself into nature. The haunting Siluetas — ephemeral outlines of the artist’s body in sand, mud, grass, fire and water — explore the indivisibility of biology and ecology, female fertility and nature’s fecundity. Shaped by exile from Cuba, Mendieta created minimal, site-specific interventions, preserved in stunningly beautiful photographs, that stand in striking contrast to the bulldozing gestures of male land artists. The result is a singular body of work that remains poetically profound and serves as a powerful reminder of humanity’s inseparability from the natural world. Read the FT’s full review

The face that launched a thousand products? Frida Kahlo might be one of the most recognisable artists today, but during her lifetime the Mexican artist worked in relative obscurity, often overshadowed by her more famous husband, Diego Rivera. In the decades since her death in 1954, however, her image has become ubiquitous, adorning everything from T-shirts and jewellery to cosmetics and souvenirs. Tate Modern traces the rise of this “Fridamania” through more than 200 commercial objects. Alongside them are 30 works by Kahlo herself and a further 200 works by later artists that reveal the lasting impact of her life, art and self-fashioning. Read the FT’s full review

From the opening moment of his rollercoaster show at the Hayward Gallery, when the monstrous PVC bulges of “All of Nothing” (2026) fill the entrance hall, balloon up to the first floor and dwarf any hope of seeing the work whole, to the rooftop apotheoses “Cloak” (2026) and “Tsunami” (2025), enormous wavy mirrors turning the gallery, London skyline and audience upside down, Anish Kapoor exuberantly challenges the South Bank’s concrete brutalism, and spins visitors into a dizzying trip through place and space, geology, biology, psychology, optics: part fairground fun, part metaphysics. Read the FT’s full review

How have people living with HIV found dignity in the face of stigma? At the Wellcome Collection, photography, film and archival material chart histories of care, activism and resistance, from the UK’s Aids epidemic in the 1990s to the present day. Highlights include images of a mass “die-in” organised by Act Up in Trafalgar Square, and Gideon Mendel’s ongoing photographic project Through Positive Eyes . Created by more than 200 participants worldwide, who were given cameras to document their everyday lives, the series offers a powerful portrait of the challenges of living with HIV, as well as the solidarity and community that can grow from shared experience.

After becoming the first French-Algerian artist to represent France at the Venice Biennale with her acclaimed 2022 presentation Dreams Have No Titles , Zineb Sedira returns with a new installation for this year’s Tate Britain Commission. Conceived as “a love letter to pan-African cinema”, “When Words Fall Silent, Cinema Speaks” transforms the neoclassical Duveen Galleries with the louche glamour of a retro film club, featuring a crimson-carpeted cinémathèque, a pop-up that simulates an Algerian café in Paris, and two new films that pay homage to African filmmakers and the history of the Cinémathèque Algérienne. Read the FT’s full interview

In this ambitious, startling, imaginatively installed show — Moore’s largest ever outdoor exhibition — the best-known British 20th-century artist manages to surprise. Throughout the gardens, the echoing of forms is a visual tease, a game of hide and seek. But there are also glaring encounters between Kew’s classical follies and Moore’s anticlassical sculptures. This is a show of depth and breadth, and will repay repeat visits as it changes with the seasons. Read the FT’s full review

To launch its latest outpost in east London, the V&A has put together an exhibition that chronicles how Black music has shaped British culture and creativity since 1900. It is emphatically vast in its scope, spanning songs of myriad genres — from 1970s lovers rock to the head-rush 1990s beats of drum ’n’ bass — artefacts, artworks and glittering fashion statements. Music is presented as a form of communication, a means of reverence and resistance as well as revelry. Read the FT’s full review

rows.title: The AI Shift: Is AI supercharging science?
rows.content:
John Burn-Murdoch and Sarah O’Connor

Published October 1 2026

This article is an on-site version of our The AI Shift newsletter. Premium subscribers can sign up here to get the newsletter delivered every Thursday. Standard subscribers can upgrade to Premium here , or explore all FT newsletters

Welcome back to The AI Shift, our weekly exploration of how AI is changing work and jobs. This week we’re digging into how AI tools are changing the way scientists carry out their research, off the back of a really interesting new study led by a team of researchers at Google.

Before we get into the findings, I want to make a meta-point. A lot of the economic research coming out of the big AI labs has focused very heavily on what their proprietary data tells them, which means we’ve had a glut of papers answering variations of the questions “what tasks are people using AI for?” and “what jobs are therefore most exposed to AI?” This is certainly useful, but it’s really only answering the first part of a much larger question of how AI is changing jobs and work. Whether using AI for a task makes the job as a whole less or more complex, less or more intense, whether it boosts productivity or simply reveals rigid bottlenecks — all of these require going a step further and looking at how workers’ use of AI for particular tasks fits into their job as a whole.

So what I really appreciated about this piece of research is that it did exactly that, combining data on how scientists are using Google’s LLM Gemini with a detailed survey of scientific researchers to paint a much fuller picture of how, where and why AI is and isn’t transforming the way science is carried out today.

Starting with the basics, the study found AI is already very heavily embedded in how scientific research is carried out. Almost half of surveyed US and UK scientists are using AI on a daily basis, and 80 per cent use it at least weekly. And by far the most common usage for LLMs and specialised models alike is to analyse or model research data.

But for me the most valuable part of the study was the additional survey data showing how this all maps onto the extensive range of tasks that make up the typical working week for a researcher, and what this means for the extent to which AI productivity gains and other benefits in one part of the job can spread to others and to the quantity and quality of scientific output more broadly. Data analysis is evidently where scientists are getting the most value from AI, but only about a fifth of their typical week is spent on analysing and interpreting data. So even full AI automation of those tasks would still leave the overall job essentially intact, and even dramatic productivity gains in the data analysis step might have a much more muted impact overall.

This is essentially what the rest of the survey results found. While the average surveyed scientist reported saving almost seven hours per week thanks to AI, only a portion of that time is being invested in starting additional research projects, and a significant amount goes on manually auditing and verifying the results of work performed by AI — what the researchers termed the “verification tax”. In addition, surveyed researchers reported that the biggest bottleneck for their overall progress is physical experiments and data collection, and that bottlenecks had moved downstream in the past two years — for example from carrying out exploratory research and analysis to doing physical lab experiments. As a result, 41 per cent of surveyed scientists said their backlog of untested theories had increased, suggesting AI is making it easier and faster to do the computational work that generates promising avenues for real-world research, but the physical world is not keeping pace, attenuating any speed-up in the overall scientific discovery process.

I should be clear that the overall sentiment from the surveyed researchers was that AI is proving very valuable to their work, and that they are bullish on its impact on tangible scientific output. But I found the nuances on lingering inefficiencies, bottlenecks and allocation of scientists’ time across tasks invaluable for thinking about how even hugely impressive AI capabilities and extensive usage can have much more modest impacts on final output than some might imagine.

Thanks John, very interesting, and some elements — like the AI “verification tax” — resonate with what we hear from other professions. I thought I’d supplement your dive into the data with some conversations with young scientists about how this actually looks and feels at the coalface (or rather, at the lab bench).

One theme that came up was the mixed blessing of AI making it easier to pursue avenues which previously might have taken months, even years, of scientific “grunt work”. Aleksy Kwiatkowski, who has finished a PhD at the University of Oxford at the intersection of machine learning and chemistry, and is about to start a job at an AI science start-up focused on the molecules generated by fungi, told me it had become important to keep an eye on the difference between “being more productive versus feeling more productive”. There is now so much information at your fingertips, he said, that it’s important to be able to “orchestrate that and understand what’s actually most useful to you.”

Wojtek Treyde, who is wrapping up a PhD (also at Oxford) on computational drug discovery, said scientists often call this ability “taste” — an admittedly “very opaque concept” which roughly means “picking the right scientific problem to work on.” (Those of you who read our newsletter a couple of weeks ago on mathematicians will recall a similar theme.)

For early-career scientists, the increased requirement for “taste” presents something of a challenge, since they don’t yet have years of experience to draw on, but Treyde reckons younger scientists also have an advantage of their own: bravery. “I think you also need [to be] bold and courageous at the same time, right?”

Meanwhile, the scientists I spoke to said the need for real-world experimentation, flagged in the Google research, helps to explain why AI hasn’t yet lived up to Silicon Valley’s breathless claims that it will “solve” all diseases. One bottleneck in the physical world? Mice. “You can’t make mice do things faster,” said Leah Morris, executive director of an organisation called Encode: AI for Science. “You can’t make them grow faster. You can’t have the virus replicate faster . . . And then the other piece is regulatory — we still have drug trials in terms of how to get things through and make them safe for humans. There are people working on how to do this more efficiently . . . but as it stands, there’s a lot that AI cannot touch.”

AI can still be transformational, though. Murray Cox, who works on cancer immunotherapies and is in the final year of a PhD at Imperial College London, told me it was important to distinguish between general-purpose LLMs and specialised models (which might not be LLMs at all) that can be built to develop a “latent understanding of data which we as scientists don’t have, or have never previously had.” Used in this way, AI “opens up a whole new door to different types of discoveries and different types of experiments”. But this often requires AI engineers to go and work in scientific labs, where “they’re able to write whole new models to develop a new layer of understanding,” as Cox put it.

And this raises another human problem: bringing the right people together. Encode: AI for Science, which Cox is also involved with, takes AI experts and plugs them into UK-based science labs (supported by UK government funding). They have also created an open-access collection of research problems proposed by academics where AI expertise is needed, in an attempt to address this “matching” bottleneck. “We had so many scientists asking us for AI talent, [and] AI talent saying, ‘Hey, I want to work on something cooler than chatbots. I want to work on something more interesting than the next tool to help your kids cheat on their homework’,” Morris explained.

Kwiatkowski and Treyde, meanwhile, are part of a group of early-career computational scientists called CompMotifs , who convene workshops and hackathons on how to build better tools for science.

In sum, the bottlenecks are real, but people are busy working on them too. And at a time when we’re hearing a lot about AI’s destructive potential, it’s heartening to remember there are a lot of smart people out there who are working thoughtfully and collaboratively to make the best of this technology. As Treyde put it: “It would be foolish to pretend there are no risks associated with AI . . . but I think at the same time this technology has huge potential right? We also should not pretend that this progress isn’t happening . . . I think it’s sort of on us to make sure that this is being used for the right things.”

Anjana Ahuja had a great piece on scientists’ fears of falling prey to “snoop-and-scoop” by AI companies (Sarah)

Stanford finance professor Hanno Lustig has a snappy read on the enormous revenues that US data centre owners will need to generate in the years ahead in order to make a positive return on their investment (John)
