rows.title: France seeks to rein in pensions and state salaries in 2027
rows.content:
Leila Abboud in Paris and Ian Smith in London

Published October 1 2026

The French government on Thursday put forward a 2027 budget with €43bn in cuts and tax rises, as it seeks to quell market jitters that have pushed the country’s borrowing costs to their highest level in almost 25 years.

The government of Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said it aimed to narrow the deficit to 5 per cent of GDP next year by slashing state spending, capping increases to pensions and civil servant salaries, while raising taxes. The French deficit is on track to rise to 5.4 per cent of GDP this year, after a deterioration in its public finances that has led to France borrowing at higher interest rates than Italy and Greece.

“We must put France back on track for deficit reduction,” said finance minister Roland Lescure. “We hope that the annus horribilis that we experienced this year will not continue.”

Lescure called on parliament to act urgently because of the ballooning interest costs. The spreads between France and other European countries must be narrowed, he said, adding that this was a “question of confidence” with markets.

Since 2024, political gridlock has made it difficult to pass budgets through a hung parliament: two of Lecornu’s predecessors were ousted by the opposition over their budget proposals. Lecornu had to agree to costly compromises to pass this year’s budget, such as rolling back an increase to the retirement age.

France’s 10-year bond yields reached as high as 4.96 per cent on Thursday, their highest point since 2002, as a global bond rout was exacerbated by investor concerns over the country’s fragile public finances. But they later fell back to 4.93 per cent in choppy trading. “Even if fully implemented, the budget would only slow the deterioration,” said ING analysts.

Investors are demanding a premium to 10-year German bonds — a key measure of investor worry — of more than 1.3 percentage points, the biggest premium since the Eurozone debt crisis.

The government said on Thursday that interest costs on French debt were expected to rise to €62.6bn this year — an increase that is higher than the entire budget of the justice ministry — and reach €91.2bn next year. France is spending more on interest than on education or defence.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The most controversial proposals are the suspension of automatic pension increases linked to rising inflation for retirees who receive more than €1,260 a month and scrapping a 10 per cent tax deduction for “professional expenses” that benefits all retirees.

“That deduction is an aberration,” given that retirees do not work, said labour minister Jean-Pierre Farandou. The pension changes would be debated with lawmakers, he added. “But it would be bizarre for the pensioners not to contribute to the collective effort” alongside workers, he said.

Overall spending on pensions will still rise given the ageing population but the increase would be reduced by about €5.5bn with the changes.

Opposition leaders such as far-right leader Marine Le Pen and far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon have already warned the government that any move to hit retirees will be unacceptable. But Le Pen has also signalled that she believes passing a budget is necessary — even if imperfect — given the potential for a debt crisis.

“The budget itself hasn’t told us much new,” said Alex Everett, a fund manager at Aberdeen Investments. “More important will be RN’s response and the ongoing debate within the French parliament.”

The government gave an overall figure of €54bn in cuts and tax revenues but that includes measures already passed in earlier budgets.

Cuts in government spending at the national and local levels would account for roughly €14bn of the savings, the government said, while excluding defence spending.

This will be Emmanuel Macron’s last budget ahead of presidential elections in April. Le Pen is topping opinion polls for the first round and she is also projected to win the run-off in several scenarios, particularly if Mélenchon makes it into the second round. Such a match-up is seen as the worst scenario for markets.

A one-time champion of business-friendly, pro-growth reforms, Macron will leave a legacy of mounting debt and gaping deficits after unfunded tax cuts and doling out aid to households and businesses in successive crises including the Covid-19 pandemic.

Macron reduced France’s headline corporate tax rate from 33.3 per cent in 2017 to 25 per cent, but successive governments have since reimposed “temporary” levies on the largest companies, pushing their combined rate to about 35 per cent.

Next year will be the fourth year running where the French deficit will be above 5 per cent of GDP, far above the EU’s cap of 3 per cent of GDP.

France has been hit with slower growth than its European counterparts this year, aggravating the deficit because of lower expected tax receipts, although inflation has trailed neighbours slightly, a relative help to consumers.

“Reducing the deficit is possible. Others have done it and we can too,” said Lescure, adding that “if we act now” brutal tax rises and cuts could be avoided.

rows.title: Burnham’s wake-up call for the right
rows.content:
Robert Shrimsley

Published October 1 2026

Timing is everything. The Labour Party has waited nearly 20 years for the type of leader Andy Burnham revealed himself to be this week, someone who could bury Blairism and still look like a winner.

There have been several false steps on the way. Gordon Brown remained troublingly committed to economics. Ed Miliband and Jeremy Corbyn could not convince the country. Keir Starmer won but then turned on the left. Burnham was rejected (twice) for still seeming too New Labour. But the pattern has been consistent: members have been willing the way back to the land before the hated neoliberalism took hold.

Now Labour has the leader it wants and at an opportune moment. Burnham can, quite clearly, do the politics and is also determined to wind back the clock. A leader who believes in higher spending, more public intervention and stronger trade unions; a leader committed to undoing Thatcherism. And above all they have him when his political opponents are in chaos.

What his bravura party conference speech ought to have rammed home to opponents is that Burnham presents an existential threat to the right of British politics and to the economic liberalism it espouses. New Andy is unapologetically old Labour and he is taking the argument for municipal socialism to an enfeebled right. And the peril for them is larger than a mere election defeat.

Alongside Burnham’s policy platform is a shrewd political strategy, calculated to rebuild the electoral coalition on the left and then drive through voting reform in the explicit belief it will keep the right out. He is planning this when, for the first time in modern politics, there is a clear split on the right which could gift him a return to Downing Street.

Consider his headline announcements of what he would do after the general election. He wants to reopen Brexit , tantalising pro-Europeans by not ruling out rejoining the EU. No doubt he is sincere, but this and his commitment to electoral reform are also calculated to tempt Lib Dems, Greens and others to lend Labour their votes.

Burnham has not committed to a specific voting system, so it is impossible to judge the impact of that intended reform. Anything close to a proportional model would mostly throw up European-style coalitions, potentially bringing left and right extremists into governing blocs.

He has spoken favourably of the supplementary vote system under which he was elected Manchester mayor. This gives voters a second preference and requires the winner to secure 50 per cent support; in many instances it will still benefit the front-running parties.

But we can be sure of two things, whatever version of electoral reform goes forward. It will not be designed to disadvantage the left and it will entrench multi-party politics, cementing the split on the right and permanently diminishing the Conservatives.

And layered on top is an economic and political argument which derides the market-based model. Perhaps this will prove mere rhetoric but the Burnham offer is to wind back the clock and, through electoral reform, to keep it there.

So his ascent should be a wake-up call to Conservatives — and all who believe in a lower-tax, smaller-state model. Labour has found a leader with the personality to offer up a left agenda to voters desperate for dramatic change and receptive to a rose-tinted view of the world before Thatcher (which three-fifths of the country will not remember).

There are two problems for Burnham. The first is that even as Labour returns to the comfort zone of what it believes to be working-class politics, the party has rarely been more middle class. A recent study showed nearly two-thirds of its voters are now economically middle class and higher. Meanwhile, working-class and non-graduate voters are moving rightward, a trend crystallised by Brexit.

The bigger obstacle is that he is still presiding over high taxes, high debt and hard times. He admits that rising energy bills will lead to a “tough winter”. Bond markets remain volatile and there is no sign of a serious plan for growth or a real roadmap to his new economy. While presenting himself as a change agent, Burnham has deferred his most transformational promises till the next election, which he claims is not soon. His gamble is that voters will keep faith till then.

But what this week has shown the right is that they now face a man who, unlike Starmer, may have the clarity of purpose and political skills to win. Burnham may still stumble. But his opponents cannot count on it.

Were they different, this would be a spur to Reform and the Tories to co-operate, but that seems highly unlikely. There is evidence it would alienate Conservative voters. With Reform a threat, left and centrist voters will bunch around Labour to stop them.

This is the reality for Kemi Badenoch as the Tory leader heads to her own party conference. Those who oppose big-state socialism have never been more in need of a strong Conservative Party and rarely further from having one. Badenoch must somehow lead an intellectual political revival with a badly discredited brand and convince voters her party is the viable alternative to Labour. This means broadening support rather than spurning liberal-minded voters.

Burnham is now offering the UK a real political fight about its future. If the right cannot regroup before he shifts the electoral rules, it will be a long road back.

rows.title: Who should pay for the LA wildfires?
rows.content:
Martha Muir in New York

Published October 1 2026

This article is an on-site version of our Energy Source newsletter. Premium subscribers can sign up here to get the newsletter delivered every Tuesday and Thursday. Standard subscribers can upgrade to Premium here , or explore all FT newsletters

Welcome to Energy Source, coming to you from New York.

A bipartisan group of US senators released a long-awaited permitting reform bill on Wednesday, which aims to speed up energy projects to meet the country’s booming demand.

Highlights of the 417-page bill text include:

The federal government can’t pull permits after September 16 2026 or prevent a permitted project from being built — unless it can prove a breach of law, fraud or new information proving harm to human life, property or national security.

The legal burden is flipped. Instead of developers having to show the government’s action was unlawful, the government would have to prove with “clear and convincing evidence” that they have a right to intervene.

If the government unlawfully intervenes, developers can claw back legal fees and delay costs plus 25 to 50 per cent of costs already incurred.

Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, he has repeatedly tried to throttle wind energy projects, including five off the US east coast and hundreds of onshore projects, invoking national security concerns that his opponents dismiss as a smokescreen for his hatred of renewable energy.

But Republicans say this goes back even further, pointing to Barack Obama and Joe Biden’s efforts to constrain fossil fuel development, including pauses on new drilling leases and LNG export approvals.

Senators Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Utah’s Mike Lee authored the bill.

“We once built projects like the Hoover Dam, the Golden Gate Bridge and the Empire State Building in years, not decades,” said Lee. “America still has the resources and the talent, but what too often stands in the way is a permitting system that takes too long and costs too much.”

Attempts to reform permitting have floundered, notably in 2022, when an attempt by senators Joe Manchin and Chuck Schumer failed due to Republican anger over the former’s role in passing the Inflation Reduction Act and Democrat concerns that it would weaken environmental protections. Even earlier this week, reports circled that language protecting offshore projects had been significantly watered down by the administration.

The bill’s fate will be decided in the lame-duck period after November’s midterm elections.

In today’s newsletter we report on California’s debate over wildfire compensation, as utilities attempt to limit their liability following last year’s blazes in Los Angeles.

Thanks for reading, Martha.

The chief executive of the California company at the centre of last year’s Los Angeles wildfires has called for a cap on utilities’ wildfire liability, warning that the current system risks the industry’s viability.

How victims of the blaze should be compensated is the subject of fierce debate in the state, with the legislature failing in September to pass new laws to determine who should pay.

A proposal from Governor Gavin Newsom, which would have shielded utilities from bankruptcy-causing costs, faced intense pushback from insurance companies and victims’ advocacy groups. The California State Assembly declined to vote on a compromise bill that would have sped up compensation for fire victims and preserved insurance companies’ right to recover costs from utilities.

Potential reforms are of great interest to Southern California Edison. Sparks from a transmission tower owned by the company have been deemed the cause of the 2025 Eaton blaze that killed 19 people and destroyed more than 9,000 homes and buildings, according to Los Angeles County fire officials.

The company faces about 2,000 lawsuits from roughly 32,000 plaintiffs.

Pedro Pizarro, chief executive of Edison International, the holding company that owns SCE, is calling for lawmakers to hold a special session before the end of the year.

“What we need is a framework that provides accountability for utility shareholders and management, to make sure we’re doing the right things,” he told Energy Source. “But if we are, then have a cap on shareholder liability. Otherwise our model is simply not viable. We can’t be an insurer of last resort.”

Concerns that California utilities will face uncapped liabilities have weighed heavily on their share prices and credit outlooks. Edison’s stock has fallen 32 per cent since the start of August, while Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E), the largest power company in the state, is down 31 per cent. Fitch downgraded SCE’s credit rating from stable to negative in September.

Pizarro says his company’s infrastructure sparking the Eaton blaze is “heartbreaking”, but a number of factors contributed to the devastation of the fire. In January SCE filed cross-claims against more than a dozen other organisations, including LA County and SoCalGas.

“When there’s a catastrophic event, the spark may come from utility equipment, but the catastrophe is much broader than that,” he said.

“You have a convergence of 100 mile-per-hour winds, lack of water availability, the winds grounding firefighting aircraft, and fire encroaching into areas that were not prepared to deal with high fire risk. As a state, our mechanisms to protect those homes that were known to be in high fire risk areas failed.”

Pizarro alleges that SoCalGas failed to carry out widespread shut-offs for four days. SoCalGas calls this an attempt to “deflect responsibility and accountability” and is pursuing recovery from SCE.

Edison says it has changed how it manages idle transmission lines after Eaton. Previously disconnected lines were grounded only at the ends. It now grounds them every two miles and is looking at whether idle lines near live high-voltage equipment should be removed. The utility says it is also improving its risk modelling.

The utilities’ attempts to limit their liability will continue to face intense pushback. The Every Fire Survivor’s Network, which says it represents more than 10,000 victims of the LA blazes, said California’s utilities had not invested enough in reducing fire risk — pointing to $500mn in wildfire mitigation funds it says Edison failed to spend.

“California does not need to restore Wall Street’s confidence in Edison and PG&E. Edison and PG&E need to earn it by making California safer,” said Joy Chen, the group’s executive director.

The group wants the state to audit utilities’ wildfire mitigation spending and for shareholders and executives to take the hit for failures.

Diesel prices will not return to normal for more than a year , according to US oil and gas executives surveyed by the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas.

Billionaire Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote said “nothing will stop” his $16bn oil refinery project from going ahead in Kenya after a court delayed the launch over a land dispute.

Battery companies want Brussels to ignore calls from carmakers and implement post-Brexit rules that would slap tariffs on most UK-EU electric car sales.

rows.title: An AI sovereign wealth fund isn’t progressive — it’s techno-imperialism
rows.content:
Evgeny Morozov

Published October 1 2026

The writer is the author of ‘The Net Delusion’ and ‘To Save Everything, Click Here’

A growing number of Americans dislike AI so Washington is trying to change their minds the old-fashioned way, with a stick and a carrot. The stick was on full display on Tuesday. President Donald Trump, with tech executives at his back, told voters that if they refuse data centres, companies will “be forced to go overseas” — and, as he put it, “whoever wins superintelligence wins . . . you’re probably not gonna have a second place” implying that detractors would be handing China victory in the AI race.

The carrot comes in the form of a dividend. In July, Sam Altman proposed that leading US AI labs each hand 5 per cent of their equity to a public fund. And Senator Bernie Sanders has introduced a bill for a national fund with 50 per cent ownership of the AI giants, with citizens entitled to a stake in their profits.

The stick, on inspection, is flimsy. The two are perfectly compatible: US-aligned data centres can go overseas while AI profits still accrue to Americans. Most of AI’s power goes into training models. This can happen wherever electricity is cheap; only the systems answering users in real time must stay near them. That means data centres can leave US soil and US companies still gain, while citizens with a stake in them are paid no matter where the machines run. For shareholders, it’s the best of both worlds: no data centre next door and a cheque in the mail.

But the machines still stand somewhere, on someone’s land, guzzling someone’s water, straining someone’s grid. Income at home from land and power abroad has an old name: empire. What’s new is the idea, shared by Altman and Sanders, of enrolling every US citizen. The result would be a new form of social and technological imperialism.

Pax Silica, the state department’s AI supply-chain club, has barely concealed its aim: to lock members into America’s compute and out of China’s. The Pentagon’s new Economic Defense Unit has even invoked the East India Company — a firm whose shareholders drew dividends from conquest — as its model. Pax Silica’s first outpost is a 4,000-acre “economic security zone” in the Philippines. Washington reportedly sought US jurisdiction and immunity for its personnel there; Manila said no twice and insists the zone will stay under Philippine law (the project is proceeding). Just as Detroit in its heyday ran on Liberian rubber and Chilean copper, San Francisco’s AI glory could run on Philippine land and other people’s megawatts.

The imperial ambition behind such initiatives has provoked discontent in host nations. In Kenya, a $1bn data centre stalled after Microsoft and its Emirati partner asked the government to guarantee purchases of its computing capacity. Mexico’s president said her country need not become the data centre of the world. What other countries cannot stop is America’s use of sanctions to lock out China by rationing advanced chips. With the US’s chips and open markets, China would crush Silicon Valley’s valuations. Shutting Beijing out allows US AI companies to capture enough profits that a public fund would be able to redistribute them. Such a fund would be no custodian of collective intelligence but a collector of geopolitical rent: the yield on keeping China’s AI down and the world’s AI bills up.

The US left seems not to have noticed. Gavin Newsom waxes lyrical about “universal basic capital”, Sanders about a Norwegian-style sovereign wealth fund. Yet, there’s a difference. Norway’s wealth comes from its own seabed, while America’s would come from a chokehold on chips and bullying weaker countries for resources. Sanders’s bill lets this slip: it traces AI’s value to humanity’s “collective intelligence”, then pays out only to Americans.

For Maga, local tribute flowing to the all-powerful centre is a cause for celebration. Not so for the left. When Edwardian social imperialists promised to fund welfare out of Pax Britannica, old socialists, from Engels to Lenin, derided workers who took the money as the labour aristocracy. Their point stands: a public that lives off the rent acquires a stake in whatever protects it.

For now, AI’s expansion abroad is a freelance affair, as individual companies cut deals that host nations can still refuse. However, once the US state clears the ground and the American public draws a dividend from it, a refusing government will find itself up against not only Washington but every American with a payout to lose.

Critics from Sanders to Steve Bannon are right about the disease: AI breeds oligarchy. But a dividend funded by flexing American muscle while underdeveloping the rest of the globe would not cure it. It would solve one injustice by hiding another, and give oligarchs what they’ve never had: a public with a stake in looking away.

A brutal sell-off in US Treasuries accelerated into the new month , driving 10-year yields to their highest since 2002 and pushing government borrowing costs around the world back to multiyear highs.

Investors warned that the $32tn US government bond market is gripped by a “vicious loop” of selling. The 10-year Treasury, the world’s most important debt market, posted its worst month in four years in September.

Yields on 10-year Treasuries topped their recent highs on Thursday, climbing 0.04 percentage points to 5.34 per cent — a level last seen almost a quarter of a century ago.

Yields on 10-year Japanese debt approached a three-decade high.

Bond markets have for months been racked by fears over the spectre of higher inflation triggered by the Middle East energy shock, but traders and investors have warned that forced selling has in recent days added to the upward pressure on Treasury yields. Yields move inversely to prices.

Thursday’s bond market sell-off came as Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, rose 2 per cent to $100 a barrel on Thursday. Oil prices and Treasuries have been in their tightest relationship since 1990 .

rows.title: We have forgotten what budgets are for
rows.content:
Martin Sandbu

Published October 1 2026

This article is an on-site version of the Free Lunch newsletter. Premium subscribers can sign up here to get the newsletter delivered every Thursday and Sunday. Standard subscribers can upgrade to Premium here , or explore all FT newsletters

Here, at last, is a Brexit benefit of sorts: UK chancellor of the exchequer John Healey’s in-tray contains only one impossible budgeting task rather than two. EU governments have not only their national budgets to worry about but face pressure to make progress on the next seven-year common budget for the bloc as a whole. This week I want to highlight a parallel between the two challenges.

The parallel is that both the UK and the EU budgets are failing badly to deliver what they are supposed to. To be sure, both public finance arrangements sustain long-established patterns of redistribution. But neither does a good job of newer and more urgent needs: in the UK, to promote higher and more productive private investment and growth, and across the EU, to fund agreed new priorities on defence, energy, industrial policy and digital technology.

The ultimate reasons for this are also similar: a set of political constraints that together make any significant change to the allocation of resources seem out of reach. In the UK, the constraints combine stultifying fiscal rules ( here is my longer take on that) and a government that thought, to be elected, it had to promise not to raise income tax, national insurance and VAT. It is therefore reduced to tweaking along the edges (and yes, I count the decision to slightly weaken the “triple lock” on state pension as no more than that).

In the EU case, the constraint takes the form of a political war of attrition. States that receive more out of the budget than they put in want to maintain the programmes that secure this. Net contributors, meanwhile, want a larger relative share to fund new priorities such as defence and energy, without increasing the overall size. Every time in the past, the result has been stalemate, last-minute brinkmanship and an outcome that only marginally changes the status quo ante. For example, researchers from Bruegel have just found that the budget currently being negotiated will only fill a small fraction of the widely recognised investment gap for European public goods.

What I think the two situations (and no doubt budgeting in many other polities) have in common is that they largely undermine the ability to use budgets as tools of governance. When politics locks public finances into at most marginal departures from the status quo, budgets cease to be tools of governance. Yet the time has long since passed when public policy could largely be left to autopilot and market equilibria.

Something has to give, and if it’s not the budgeting process, it’s most likely a crisis that ultimately forces politicians’ hands. The much better alternative is to find a way to deliberately unlock the political economy of budgeting. That is easy to say, of course, and harder to figure out how to do. But if we know that moving incrementally means hardly moving at all, then it’s at least clear that much bigger steps are needed: these are chasms that cannot be crossed in many small leaps. So what might this entail for the two cases I have mentioned?

In the UK, it is surely a comprehensive reform of the entire tax system. My colleague Martin Wolf wrote this week that: “The important challenge is to improve the efficiency of the fiscal system . . . [D]o not look at a single tax on its own but relative to the rest. The time now is ripe for such reform.” What sort of reform? He rightly points out that a comprehensive overhaul needs to be done with deliberation and care, and mentions the 2011 Mirrlees Review , which remains as good a place as any to start.

But it is possible to state straightforwardly what one thinks should be the main steps of a good reform. As I have written before, I think a lot would be gained from fully harmonising the taxation of income, replacing the current income tax and employers’ national insurance, as well as capital income taxation, with a single new tax that would cover all sources at the same rates for the same levels of income. This would have some obvious losers: those with non-labour income, where national insurance is not paid today, and those with capital gains, who would no longer pay lower tax than wage earners. But that could in return pay for noticeably lower rates.

For example: based on Resolution Foundation research , shifting 2 percentage points from employee national insurance (which is not paid on pensions and investment incomes) to income tax (which is) would raise £6bn. So a rough estimate is that folding the entire 8 per cent national insurance into income tax would give the government roughly £25bn to play with. New research from CenTax , meanwhile, finds that taxing capital gains like other sources of income would raise an additional £20bn. Add in other, smaller effects, and the amounts raised easily surpass £50bn a year. And that is before even contemplating similar simplifying reforms to VAT or property taxation.

The point is not that taxes should rise by that amount, but to underline just how much political room for manoeuvre comprehensive reform buys you. With these sorts of resources, a lot of taxes can be cut. For about £10bn a year , the threshold for paying tax on income at all could be unfrozen, along with that for the higher rate. For about the same amount , you could cut all income tax rates or VAT by 1 percentage point, or corporation tax by 2.5 percentage points. (All of which should be good for growth.) It would be a poor politician who could not marshal that kind of largesse into political support. As an added benefit, if income tax and national insurance no longer existed in their previous forms, it’s not clear how Labour’s manifesto pledge not to raise their rates would continue to bind.

One could mount all kinds of objections. But the question really is: who can honestly say the current marginalist approach to budgeting is delivering?

What about the EU? There, the political economy deadlock may seem deeper than in the UK. It is caused not by the self-imposed strictures of an otherwise all-powerful one-party government, but by the irreconcilable policy positions of many veto players. Not literally irreconcilable — every seven years, EU leaders somehow hammer out a compromise and pass a budget, but always involving very small changes. Irreconcilable, then, in that it seems impossible to get much past the status quo ante.

Here too, it is useful to think about how root-and-branch reform could change the political economy of budgeting. How, when unanimity is so hard to get to? But this objection assumes that a budget must be agreed. That is not true. EU law provides that without a budget agreement, previous spending decisions are carried on. The nominal spending limits follow a fixed 2 per cent inflation adjustment — so as long as nominal growth exceeds that, the share of the budget to GDP will keep shrinking.

So consider a radical rupture with current procedures, in which EU leaders simply decided not to agree a new budget. (Unanimity means it only takes one brave leader to impose this on the rest . . . ) The status quo ante would prevail, but be eroded by inflation and growth over time. That erosion is sizeable. (For illustration: in the soon-to-be finished seven-year budgetary period, EU nominal GDP has gone up by about 40 per cent. Against a 2 per cent per year inflation adjustment, that sort of increase would shrink the budget as a share of GDP by more than one-fifth.) In isolation, this is a double win for the net contributors, who would contribute less and less overall, and in particular cut the size of the traditional transfers they most object to. That alone should concentrate the minds of net recipients.

Another consequence, however, would be resources falling even more glaringly short of what is required for new, geopolitically important spending. So in this hypothetical world where budget talks both consumed a lot less political attention and evidently did not address agreed priorities, the pressure would rise to come up with other solutions — parallel budgets, as it were.

The EU has a good record of coming up with these quickly when needed. Most notable is NextGenerationEU , agreed within months during the Covid-19 pandemic and largely matching the normal seven-year budget for size. Sure, an unemployment reinsurance scheme, Safe, a fund for joint defence procurement, and the Ukraine Support Loan as well as earlier facilities to fund Kyiv through joint debt, together committed nearly another seven-year budget’s worth of resources. The USL even pioneered a way to borrow jointly against the EU’s creditworthiness while leaving some unwilling countries off the hook through side payments.

This is beginning to look like a political economy to produce a shrinking traditional budget coupled with more — and more debt-funded — new budgets for specific purposes. Does anyone think the current model — which wastes enormous amounts of time and effort and by common consent fails to address the most urgent priorities — is preferable?

rows.title: Flydubai scare revives Israel’s hijacking trauma
rows.content:
Mehul Srivastava and Peter Campbell in London and Neri Zilber in Tel Aviv

Published October 1 2026

For Israelis watching the emergency landing of Flydubai flight 1073 on Wednesday, the events of the attack echoed a painful history of aircraft hijackings.

Between 1968 and 1986, Palestinian militants hijacked or attempted to take over at least a dozen planes. Many of the attacks were supported by leftist groups in Europe and elsewhere.

The impetus for the chaos on board the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv is still unknown. The United Arab Emirates on Thursday said it was investigating whether the attack — in which one pilot assaulted the other in an apparent attempt to crash the plane — was premeditated or connected to “terrorist activity”.

Authorities have not so far labelled it a hijacking, although the aircraft issued a 7500 code that is used in such incidents.

Among the most infamous hijackers of past decades was Leila Khaled, the Palestinian militant who orchestrated the 1969 takeover of a TWA flight from Rome to Tel Aviv, forcing the pilot at gunpoint to fly to Damascus instead.

That hijacking heralded years of headline-grabbing assaults on commercial flights and civilians connected to Israel. Planes were often diverted to airfields in hostile countries, and their passengers were swapped for mostly Palestinian prisoners.

Three men affiliated with the leftist Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine hijacked a Rome-Tel Aviv flight and diverted it to Algiers, triggering a 40-day hostage crisis that ended with a swap of 16 Palestinian prisoners for a dozen Israeli men.

Three aircraft were simultaneously taken over by PFLP militants, two of them flown to Dawson’s Field in Jordan and one to Cairo. Mostly Israeli and male Americans were held hostage, and later swapped for four PFLP prisoners, including Leila Khaled.

A Frankfurt-bound flight was hijacked after taking off from Damascus, then forced to circle Zagreb airport with little remaining fuel until German authorities agreed to free the three surviving perpetrators of the Munich Olympics massacre of Israeli athletes earlier that year.

In 1976, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s brother Yoni was killed while rescuing more than 100 remaining predominantly Israeli and Jewish hostages from an Air France flight that had been hijacked and flown to Uganda, and welcomed by the dictator Idi Amin.

In 1972, three members of the Japanese Red Army shot and killed 26 people at Lod airport in Israel.

Another hijacking attempt took place in 1986, when militants took over a Pan Am flight and demanded the freedom of Palestinian prisoners.

Little is known about the assailant aboard the Flydubai flight, though Israeli authorities have said he was Omani. After speaking to Netanyahu on Wednesday, Donald Trump said it remained unclear whether the pilot was “a terrorist or perhaps a whackjob”.

In recent decades, Israelis have grown accustomed to an extra-vigilant system of protecting planes, especially for the national flag carrier El Al.

Many added security measures were designed to stop hijackers from sneaking themselves and their weapons on board.

Some of the biggest changes to aeroplanes globally were made after 9/11, when more cockpit locks were added. Israeli carriers had started the process earlier, including with steps to make sure would-be hijackers would not be able to shoot through the cockpit door, said a veteran of the Israeli aviation security industry.

“Israel was the pioneer in the field” of aviation security, going back to the early 1970s, he said. Israel was the first to introduce a security protocol, including questioning passengers ahead of boarding, checking hand luggage and placing air marshals on flights.

Cockpit doors were also equipped with a mechanism that meant the door could be opened only from the inside or with a code given to the cabin crew.

The in-flight cockpit visits that were previously granted to flying enthusiasts, airline regulars or excited small children were also banished.

“For all the security theatre that 9/11 brought into play, the single most effective thing we did was harden the cabin door and make it impossible for others to get into the cockpit,” said Andrew Charlton, a former aviation executive who now leads the Aviation Advocacy consultancy.

While these measures have prevented some incidents, they have enabled others. The Germanwings 9525 crash in 2015 came after one pilot took control of the plane and dived into the French Alps while the other was locked out.

For Israel, the hijackings of the 1970s and 1980s were followed by decades of investment in the security of their airports, namely Ben Gurion near Tel Aviv.

After 9/11, western governments demanded airports around the world comply with rigorous safety checks in order to be certified to fly into major hubs.

El Al is considered by analysts to be among the most security-conscious of all national carriers, with intensive — and often invasive — checks for passengers. It is often criticised for racially profiling Palestinian and non-Jewish travellers. But the Israeli airline’s planes are “like Fort Knox”, says Charlton.

After a 2002 attempt to shoot down an Israeli plane in Kenya, custom modifications were made to El Al planes that allowed them to shoot flares to divert incoming heat-seeking missiles.

Passengers from the Flydubai flight diverted to Saudi Arabia arrive at Israel's Ben Gurion airport

That system was later replaced by one that used lasers to jam the ability of so-called MANPADs — shoulder-mounted missile systems — to lock on to the aircraft even before they were fired.

El Al planes on the ground are guarded at all times, including overnight. A large proportion of its pilots are retired Israeli Air Force veterans, and each plane carries at least two, if not more, armed air marshals, according to current and former pilots for the airline.

When the airline launches to a new destination, the host airport usually has to make security improvements. When flights to Geneva started, a new set of doors was installed to prevent anything being thrown directly into the buildings.

But despite the ever-ratcheting changes, analysts and executives acknowledge that the race to prevent would-be attackers is never finished.

“It is the sad truth that aviation security has to be lucky every single time, they only have to be lucky once,” said Charlton. “We are constantly catching the last one, not the next one.”

rows.title: Wachtell hires former Manhattan US attorney to strengthen litigation ranks
rows.content:
Sujeet Indap in London and Oliver Barnes in New York

Published October 1 2026

Legal powerhouse Wachtell Lipton is hiring the former chief US prosecutor in Manhattan to bolster the ranks of its litigation practice after the shock departure of its top trial lawyer earlier this year.

Joon Kim made his name as a prosecutor in two stints at the US attorney’s office in Manhattan, one of the justice department’s most powerful prosecutorial offices. He is joining Wachtell from rival firm Cleary Gottlieb, where he started his career as a junior associate and most recently served an eight-year stint as a litigation partner.

“My goal has been to practise law at the highest level,” Kim told the FT in an interview. “I think of Wachtell Lipton as the standard that other law firms measure themselves against.”

The hire marks a rare move by Wachtell to poach talent from a rival and follows the June departure of Bill Savitt , the co-chair of the firm’s executive committee and head litigator, alongside five other partners for rival Gibson Dunn.

Until recently, Wachtell, known for its high pay and prestige, had avoided losing talent to other firms , but the pace of Wachtell partner defections has accelerated in recent years amid a heated transfer market for top legal talent.

Wachtell, whose core strength is its M&A advisory practice, also maintains a focused but high-powered litigation practice to complement its corporate deal work. Most recently, Wachtell led the investigation, commissioned by the NBA, into salary cap misconduct allegations involving the Los Angeles Clippers franchise.

Kim will join as a partner, working on high-stakes litigation, enforcement and white-collar crime matters. Wachtell has roughly 20 litigation partners, compared with 35 corporate partners.

“Joon is a terrific cultural fit and we are thrilled he has chosen to join us,” Wachtell said in statement.

His tenure in the Manhattan federal prosecutor’s office included several high-level postings, including chief of the Southern District of New York criminal division and deputy US attorney.

Kim was a senior official in the office as it pursued wrongdoing allegations against Steven Cohen’s SAC Capital Advisors, which eventually pleaded guilty to a securities fraud charge and paid a $1.8bn fine, and the high-profile case against Ross Ulbricht, the founder of online black-market enterprise Silk Road. After then-Manhattan US attorney Preet Bharara was fired by the Trump administration in 2017, Kim served as the interim head prosecutor in the office, in effect acting as Wall Street’s top cop for the ensuing 10 months. As acting US attorney, he oversaw the prosecution of the professional gambler Billy Walters in an insider-trading ring.

Since joining Cleary, Kim has represented the likes of Nissan and Sequoia Capital. Kim was also hired in 2021 by the New York state attorney-general to investigate multiple sexual harassment allegations against then-governor Andrew Cuomo, an inquiry that ultimately led to Cuomo’s resignation.

rows.title: The awesome appeal of aso oke, and other Nigerian ceremonial robes
rows.content:
Dal Chodha

Published October 1 2026

In 2020, Michelle Adepoju was on the hunt for weavers who could make fabrics for her fledgling fashion label Kílèntár. Searching her hometown of Ondo in south-west Nigeria, the London- and Lagos-based designer uncovered something revelatory. Among the market stalls selling old sewing machines, lace and wooden carvings, Adepoju found vintage pieces of aso oke, a handwoven textile originating from the Yoruba people. Traditionally worn as part of outfits for special occasions, each piece of varying length has a graphic pattern typically formed of tightly woven lines, jagged grids and bold arrows. Adepoju immediately felt a kinship. “It was like gold to me,” she says. “I knew it had value.” Adepoju bought them up, beginning a collection that now includes more than 500 pieces, some dating back as far as the 1940s.

c1900 silk wrapper, £675 at Adire African Textiles

c1978 cotton and Lurex aso oke from the British Museum’s collection

She started upcycling vintage aso oke fabrics into wearable wide-leg trousers and evening dresses for Kílèntár , but stopped when she realised the educational value of what she had amassed. In December, she opened a bright white retail space in Lagos , placing her strapless minidresses, corsets and cargo pants among wall hangings made up of 200 patchworked lengths of aso oke. Examples around 2sq m sell for £8,000 and are accompanied by a booklet detailing the material’s provenance. At home she displays more precious and personal pieces on shelves.

Aso oke has, thus far, been relatively under-appreciated on the secondary market. “The techniques of making textiles here were not shared outside of the country so it is little known around the world and many of the older weavers and their techniques have now passed on. Africans know this history already and they don’t value it so much,” says dealer Alhaji Salami, who has assisted Adepoju in building her collection. Adepoju concurs: “Yet in the west, people are seeing that it has heritage, it has importance.” Duncan Clarke, founder of Adire African Textiles, began trading in the late ’90s using cloths he’d gathered while researching his PhD in Yoruba textiles. In the academic field of African art, textiles have always been something of a poor relation to masks and sculpture, he says. Collectors are “less interested in textiles with the exception of kuba raffia, which sneaks into the edge of the canon because Matisse liked them”.

For Adepoju, showing them in her house and her shop has become a way for her to explore Nigerian artisanal knowledge and to share that with a generation of young Africans. “I think people are filled with awe, wondering how this could have been made by hand, with a single needle, more than 100 years ago,” says Salami.

Kílẹ̀ńtàr vintage patchwork wall hanging, £2,500

c1930s cotton Yoruba aso oke wrap cloth, sold for £375 at Adire African Textiles

c1900 handspun cotton and silk aso oke from the collection of the British Museum

c1970 Yoruba aso oke wrap cloth, sold for £340 at Adire African Textiles

There are three archetypal types of aso oke, which means “top cloth”: sanyan, which is an earthy beige colour, the indigo etu and alaari, a bright magenta – all usually woven in cotton. “Some of the dyes are from the soil, or from leaves or the dust from the roadside,” says Salami, who spends most of his time travelling to Togo, Côte d’Ivoire and Burkina Faso in search of aso oke for his global clients.

Collectors should feel for the quality of the fabric when starting out. “Quality does decline over time,” Clarke says. “Early pieces were made in handspun cotton and silk that came from the trans-Saharan trade.”

Nzuri Textiles, based in the Sierra foothills of northern California, is listing a soft-brown sanyan cloth from Oyo state dating back to the 1930s. The Niger Bend – also in the US – has a range of small pieces: it recently sold a repeat misstep pattern cloth for £136, and has a larger fine-gauge blue-and-white cotton cloth that has been tightly woven on a traditional double-heddle dragstone loom by accomplished Yoruba male weavers for about £223.

Pieces from the past 40 years can be a good starting point. “As the 20th century went on, silk dropped out but they still used the colour from Manchester silk merchants along with nylon. A greater range of colours came in by the 1960s and then Lurex,” says Clarke. On Etsy a length of cream aso oke with stripes of brown and wine-red running through, dating from the 1940s, is £130.

But “the old ones are the real aso oke”, Salami concludes. “Etu translates as ‘fear’ in Yoruba. Our forefathers believed that when you have the etu fabrics in your house, then any sickness or stress will not enter. Many of the fabrics have these beliefs attached to them. That’s what gives them their value too.”

rows.title: Music Thing’s compact synth will make a composer out of you
rows.content:
Rhodri Marsden

Published October 1 2026

Music Thing Workshop System Price: £750 BUY

Learning to play an instrument tends to follow a well-worn path: get to grips with technique, play your first notes or rhythms and gently ease yourself into the western musical tradition. Music Thing’s Workshop System – a compact, keyboard-less synthesiser in a small, foam-lined case – sets all that aside and asks you merely to have fun with sound by connecting its various modules. Turn knobs, flick switches, create some noise, listen to it metamorphose and make soundscapes as smooth or as jagged as you like.

It’s the brainchild of Tom Whitwell, a former magazine editor at Mixmag and The Face . For years he’d been tinkering with DIY electronics and modular synthesisers while running a blog documenting his work. When he was asked to run a week-long retreat focused on sound experimentation, he came up with a rough design for a compact, all-in-one instrument that could be played by anyone, not just synth nerds. “We’d start with a simple sine wave, play with that for a while,” he says, describing a typical workshop. “Then connect to the frequency modulator, turn the control – and the noise becomes bonkers, everyone just starts laughing! People play with it in a way that I find so interesting, because there’s no right and wrong.”

Music Thing's Workshop System in action

A light-touch manual gives you enough information to get started, but the key is experimentation. Plug in a pair of headphones and use the supplied 3.5mm jack cables to connect oscillators to filters and modulators, turning knobs and learning what each of them does while creating a fizzing whoosh or a growling resonant loop. The system is augmented by tiny add-on cards that pop in a slot and let you incorporate everything from bell-ringing sequences to the sound of rain. While to some degree you’re wrestling with the machine’s idiosyncrasies, using it is analogous to singing, because you’re responding intuitively to what you hear. I’m a classically trained musician who’s been a slave to the 12-note scale for nearly my whole life, and I’ve lost hours to this thing. It’s like being a kid again.

AlphaTheta XDJ-AN DJ system Price: £999 BUY

DJing journeys often begin with a simple controller with decks and faders that operates software running on a laptop. This portable, all-in-one system dispenses with the laptop entirely; it has a built-in screen and can pull in tracks from a USB stick, Rekordbox Cloud or a streaming subscription (Apple Music, Beatport or Tidal), letting you construct playlists on the fly and quickly assign tracks to each deck. I particularly liked the coloured waveforms that identify upcoming bass-heavy (or bass-light) sections of music, the ability to use effects (filter, echo, reverb) to smooth transitions, and millisecond-perfect looping of sections. With a layout inspired by club-standard units, it offers a significant step-up for bedroom DJs.

Musical Beings Tembo Price: POA BUY

Much modern music-making happens in a grid, prodding at dots on a screen to create beats and sequences. Tembo turns this into a supremely tactile process, with a wooden chequerboard-style matrix, built-in speakers and beats (wooden discs) that are magnetically held in place. Move a “beat” across the board and the rhythm changes. Stacking them or flipping them over introduces variation. A music teacher friend of mine remarked that it has huge potential for teaching rhythm to kids, but it’s also a powerful musical tool, with a sampler, filter and effects along with USB connectivity to other MIDI instruments. Tembo smashed through its Kickstarter target almost 50 times over, and the waiting list is open for its second round of shipping.

Enya Cyber-G Pocket instrument Price: £199 BUY

Folded, it looks like a Bluetooth speaker – and it is. Unfolded, it looks like a handheld metal detector wielded at airport security, but it’s actually a neat portable instrument that’s playable by musical novices. You hold it like a guitar, pressing pads on the “fretboard” while thumbing a single trigger switch to produce beautifully voiced guitar or piano chords. It doesn’t take much exploration to figure out how to play a simple song (say, The Beatles’ “Let It Be”), but connect it to the accompanying app and you can change sounds, key, beats, tempo, and play along to a library of songs, guided by flashing lights on the neck. Or you can change all the preset chords, choose a distorted guitar sound and go full jazz metal.

Fraknoise Melancholytron Price: €825 BUY

Dutch multimedia artist Allard Krijger has long had a fascination with the idea of melancholy, and his latest exploration of the theme is a 72-page book of art, poetry and prose that comes with a synthesiser. In Krijger’s words, “it allows you to hear and perhaps play melancholy… each sound an attempt to capture a particular shade” – be that nostalgic, urban or romantic. Its various sounds are listed in the book, and while their names don’t give much clue as to their nature (“Liminale”, “Greylorn”) the idea is that you explore them through play, with different key combinations shifting the mood. The sonic quality is reminiscent of the ’60s mellotron beloved by Krijger, but he created all the sounds from scratch. A unique project.

rows.title: Starbucks opens first cafés in China’s troubled Xinjiang
rows.content:
Edward White in Shanghai

Published October 1 2026

Starbucks has opened its first cafés in China’s Xinjiang region, in a high-profile expansion by one of the world’s best-known consumer brands into an area that has attracted international concern over the repression of Uyghurs and other Muslim minority groups.

Chinese state media this week heralded the US coffee giant’s opening of two new stores in the regional capital of Ürümqi — one at the airport and another at the city’s famous Grand Bazaar. It noted both stores had “locally inspired” menus, including salty milk tea, and the bazaar store has “ Xinjiang elements” including ethnic musical instruments.

Starbucks , which opened its first store in China in 1999, is following dozens of international brands that have poured money into the region . Investment by companies such as Accor, Hilton, IHG, Marriott and Wyndham is aimed at capturing a slice of the region’s domestic tourism boom.

International hotel operators have more than 50 properties under construction or in planning in the region, expanding from 163 already in operation.

The investment push comes against a backdrop of a US-led sanctions regime that was introduced in the wake of the state’s mass detention of mainly Muslim Uyghurs and other minorities in the 2010s.

Molly Liu, chief executive officer of Starbucks China, said in a statement: “Entering Xinjiang not only marks a further expansion of our store network, but also allows us to engage deeply with this vibrant market and build sincere, lasting connections with our customers there.”

Starbucks last year agreed to sell a majority stake in its China business to private equity group Boyu Capital to form a joint venture valued at $4bn, aiming to more than double its 8,000 stores in the country of 1.4bn people.

This month, the Global Times, a Chinese Communist Party mouthpiece, said that Xinjiang registered a 22 per cent year-on-year increase in newly established foreign-funded enterprises last year, while foreign investment was up nearly 10 per cent.

“Foreign investors have made their choices, as international brands have continued to enter Xinjiang despite the unfounded accusations from the west,” the paper said.

According to official Chinese data, Xinjiang received 323mn tourist visits in 2025, up 8 per cent from the year prior. These visits generated spending of $52bn.

In 2022, following a landmark investigation, the UN’s top human rights body concluded that a “pattern of large-scale arbitrary detention occurred” in Xinjiang that could constitute “crimes against humanity”.

The Chinese government has long defended the security crackdown as a necessary response to terrorism and religious extremism. It has denied the alleged “crimes against humanity” and claims of ongoing repression in the region.

Maya Wang, deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch, a US-based NGO, said Starbucks was opening in a region where hundreds of thousands of Uyghurs remained in prison because of their ethnic and religious identity. She believed authorities had sought to “cover up” human rights abuses by presenting “a veneer of normalcy”.

“The presence of Starbucks in Xinjiang’s streets thus fits in the party-state’s narrative that there’s nothing wrong about the region to the outside world,” she said.

Asked about such concerns, a Starbucks spokesperson in China said: “Every Starbucks coffeehouse, wherever it is located, operates under the same Starbucks brand standards and values, including those related to responsible business practices.”
